paras.la: DIRECTORIUM EXERCITIORUM SPIRITUALIUM P. N. Ignatii. IHS. Florentiae, apud Philippum Iunctam, M.D.IC.
paras.en: DIRECTORY OF THE SPIRITUAL EXERCISES of Our Father Ignatius. IHS. Florence, at the press of Filippo Giunta, 1599.

paras.la: Directorium exercitiorum spiritualium ante aliquot annos typis excusum eo consilio ad Provincias missum fuit, ut antequam suprema manus operi imponeretur, usus atque experientia docerent, an aliquid addi, aut detrahi, vel etiam commodius dici posse videretur: atque in hunc finem omnes monuimus, ut si alicui tale quidpiam occurreret, per suos superiores ad R. P. N. Generalem Romam mitteret. Cum autem quaedam a nonnullis observata, ac Romam transmissa fuissent, iis omnibus in quinta Congregatione Generali a Deputatis Patribus ad Directorium recognoscendum diligenter, atque exacte discussis, iterumque a R. P. N. Patribusque Assistentibus accurate perpensis, ad hunc tandem modum Directorium accommodari posse visum est: speramusque laborem hunc non solum probatum iri, sed etiam iis qui spiritualia exercitia tradituri sunt valde utilem fore. Reliquum est, ut hac occasione nostri (ut plenius ad Provinciales communibus literis scriptum est) in posterum ad exercitia spiritualia frequentanda studiosius incumbant, et aliis etiam maiori cum utilitate tradere studeant. Datum Romae Calendis Octobris 1599. Mandato R. P. N. Generalis. Iacobus Dominicus Secretarius.
paras.en: The Directory of the Spiritual Exercises, printed some years ago, was sent to the Provinces with this intention: that before the final hand was laid to the work, use and experience might teach whether anything ought to be added or removed, or might be said more suitably. To that end we advised everyone that if any such point occurred to anyone, he should send it through his superiors to Our Father General at Rome. When certain observations from a number of persons had been transmitted to Rome, all of these were carefully and exactly discussed at the Fifth General Congregation by the Fathers deputed to revise the Directory, and were again weighed with care by Our Father General and the Father Assistants; and it was judged that the Directory could at last be settled in the present form. We hope this labour will not only meet with approval, but will also be of great use to those who are to give the Spiritual Exercises. It remains that on this occasion our men (as has been written more fully to the Provincials in a common letter) should henceforth apply themselves more earnestly to the frequent practice of the Spiritual Exercises, and take pains to give them to others with the greater profit. Given at Rome on the first of October, 1599. By order of Our Father General. Giacomo Domenici, Secretary.

vorspann.label: Prooemium
vorspann.la_titel: Prooemium: de dignitate et utilitate Exercitiorum, et de necessitate Directorii
vorspann.en_titel: Proem: on the dignity and usefulness of the Exercises, and on the need for a Directory

paras.la: Inter alia instrumenta, quae Deus pro sua bonitate ac clementia Societati nostrae, tum ad propriam, tum ad proximorum salutem perfectionemque procurandam largiri dignatus est, non postremum locum habent spiritualia exercitia.
paras.en: Among the instruments which God in his goodness and mercy has deigned to bestow on our Society for procuring both our own salvation and perfection and that of our neighbours, the Spiritual Exercises hold no last place.

paras.la: Haec enim sunt spiritualia quaedam documenta, quae, ut in huius libri praefatione dicitur, non tam ex libris, quam ex unctione Spiritus Sancti, et ex interna experientia et usu, noster in Christo Pater Ignatius composuit. Haec sunt lumina, quae ei Dominus in ipso primo conversionis fervore inspiravit, ac deinde in omni progressu eius virtutis et sanctitatis semper confirmavit.
paras.en: For these are spiritual teachings which, as is said in the preface of this book, our Father in Christ Ignatius composed not so much from books as from the anointing of the Holy Spirit and from inward experience and practice. These are the lights which the Lord inspired in him in the very first fervour of his conversion, and afterwards confirmed throughout the whole progress of his virtue and holiness.

paras.la: Quemadmodum igitur Dominus Deus ideam totam Societatis nostrae, tum exteriorem, tum etiam quae ad interiorem virtutum formam pertineret, ei tanquam capiti et fundatori communicavit, ita etiam, cum oratio et communicatio cum Deo sit tanti momenti, ut magna ex parte religiosa observantia ac spiritualis profectus ex ea pendeat, plurimum referebat habere hanc methodum et directionem ad orationem faciendam ab eodem Capite nostro, quam nos quoque omnes sequeremur, et prae oculis semper habere conaremur.
paras.en: As the Lord God communicated the whole idea of our Society — both its outward form and what belongs to the inward form of its virtues — to him as its head and founder, so too, since prayer and communication with God are of such moment that religious observance and spiritual progress depend on them in great part, it mattered greatly to have from that same head of ours this method and direction for making prayer, which we also should all follow and strive to keep always before our eyes.

paras.rub: Usus Exercitiorum a S. P. N. magnopere commendatus
paras.la: Atque haec causa est, cur ipse P. N. Ignatius in omni sermone, ut accepimus, et vero praxi ipsa tantopere nostris commendare soleret usum horum exercitiorum; ac in Constitutionibus quoque tam crebro eorum mentionem faciat, et praesertim parte 4, cap. 8, § 5, ubi dicitur, omnes operam dare debere, ut in hoc armorum spiritualium genere tractando, quod tantopere conferre cernitur ad Dei obsequium, dexteritatem habeant. Extat etiam eius epistola ad sacerdotem quendam, Mionam nomine, qui Parisiis fuerat eius confessarius, in qua satis manifeste ostendit, quid ille sentiret de his exercitiis. Monet enim eum atque etiam instanter rogat, ut ea faciat diligenter, et si fecerit, promittit ei magnam utilitatem spiritualem, tum in se ipso, tum ad alios quam plurimos iuvandos, idque verbis valde gravibus et significantibus.
paras.en: And this is the reason why Our Father Ignatius himself, in all his conversation, as we have received, and indeed in his very practice, used so greatly to commend to our men the use of these Exercises; and why in the Constitutions too he mentions them so often, above all in Part IV, chapter 8, § 5, where it is said that all should take pains to acquire skill in handling this kind of spiritual weaponry, which is seen to contribute so much to the service of God. There also survives his letter to a certain priest named Miona, who had been his confessor at Paris, in which he shows plainly enough what he thought of these Exercises: he admonishes him, and even urgently begs him, to make them diligently, and promises him, if he does, great spiritual profit, both in himself and for the helping of very many others — and this in words of great weight and significance.

paras.la: Idem vero testimonium dederunt alii, et plurimi, et quidam insignes viri, et doctrina, et virtute, et rerum humanarum experientia, ac praecipue etiam spiritualium peritia: qui cum haec exercitia re ipsa experti essent, ita ea probarunt, ut illorum usu maiorem quam sperare ausi essent suarum animarum fructum se consecutos esse tum verbo, tum scripto libenter praedicarent.
paras.en: The same testimony has been given by others — very many, and some of them distinguished men in learning, in virtue, in experience of human affairs, and above all in skill in things spiritual. Having tried these Exercises in actual fact, they so approved them that they gladly proclaimed, both by word and in writing, that by their use they had gathered a greater fruit for their souls than they had dared to hope.

paras.la: Sed prae omnibus est auctoritas Sedis Apostolicae, quae diligenti examine doctorum virorum praemisso haec exercitia approbavit anno 1548, ut pietate et sanctitate plena (haec enim sunt eius verba) et ad aedificationem spiritualemque fidelium profectum valde utilia.
paras.en: But above all stands the authority of the Apostolic See, which, after a careful examination by learned men, approved these Exercises in the year 1548 as full of piety and holiness (for these are its words) and as very useful for the edification and spiritual progress of the faithful.

paras.la: Postremo est etiam ipsa experientia ingentis ac prope incredibilis utilitatis, quae ex his exercitiis facientis subsequi solet. Primum enim plurimi ex nostris, praesertim primis temporibus, hoc modo spiritum vocationis acceperunt, ut vere dici possit Societatem nostram hoc maxime medio et initio coaluisse et postea incrementum accepisse. Deinde plurimi etiam alii, relicto mundo, alios religiosos ordines ingressi sunt; multi iam ingressi egregie reformati sunt, nec singuli tantum, sed saepe integra coenobia. Complures etiam in saeculo ipso, cum ita vitiis addicti essent, ut nullo modo neque cohortationibus neque concionibus avelli possent, hoc uno sese converterunt, et ad meliorem vitam constanter ducendam revocarunt. Denique negari non potest, quin valde magnus fructus in omni hominum genere, et statu, et conditione effectus sit, et ubi eorum usus magis viget, ibi etiam multo maior morum reformatio cernitur.
paras.en: Lastly there is experience itself of the immense and almost incredible profit that usually follows for the one who makes these Exercises. First, very many of ours, especially in the first years, received the spirit of their vocation in this way — so that it can truly be said that our Society grew together at its beginning chiefly by this means, and afterwards received its increase. Then very many others, leaving the world, entered other religious orders; many already in religion were notably reformed — and not individuals only, but often whole monasteries. Not a few, too, remaining in the world, though so given over to vices that they could in no way be torn from them by exhortations or by sermons, were converted by this one means and brought back to leading, with constancy, a better life. Finally it cannot be denied that a very great fruit has been wrought in every kind, state and condition of men; and where the use of the Exercises flourishes more, there a far greater reformation of conduct is also to be seen.

paras.la: Nec debet aliquis mirari quod tanti effectus consequantur, et quidem non admodum longo tempore — addo etiam, non adeo magno labore. Nam cum Dei voluntas sit sanctificatio nostra, ut ait Apostolus (1 Thess. 4, 3), et ideo bonitas illa immensa semper parata sit sua dona effundere super creaturam suam, sine dubio, si ipsamet non poneret impedimentum, sed potius seipsam disponeret, facile ac brevi magnas a Deo gratias consequeretur. Hoc igitur faciunt haec exercitia, et sane valde efficaciter, ut animam disponant ad haec dona accipienda. Primum enim removent eam ab omni aliarum rerum ac negotiorum occupatione, et quasi ad solitudinem quandam ducunt, ut et Deus ad eius cor loquatur, et ipsa faciat quod dicitur in Psalmo: Vacate, et videte quoniam ego sum Deus (Ps. 45, 11). Deinde vero, posito statim ante oculos ultimo hominis fine, nempe aeterna beatitudine, ostendunt primum quantum hactenus aberraverit, et ita peccatorum dolorem et odium ingenerant; deinde virtutum pulchritudinem aperiunt, et Christi Domini exemplo ad eius imitationem accendunt. Denique etiam modum tradunt totius vitae ex Dei regula ac voluntate reformandae, sive status ipse mutandus sit, sive non mutandus, verum in melius corrigendus.
paras.en: Nor should anyone wonder that such effects follow, and that in no very long time — I add, with no very great labour. For since the will of God is our sanctification, as the Apostle says (1 Thess 4:3), and that immense goodness is therefore always ready to pour out its gifts upon its creature, there is no doubt that if the soul itself did not put an obstacle in the way, but rather disposed itself, it would easily and quickly obtain great graces from God. This, then, is what these Exercises do, and most effectively: they dispose the soul to receive these gifts. For first they withdraw it from all occupation with other things and affairs, and lead it as it were into a certain solitude, so that God may speak to its heart, and it may do what is said in the Psalm: Be still, and see that I am God (Ps 45:11). Then, setting at once before its eyes the last end of man — eternal blessedness — they show it first how far it has hitherto gone astray, and so beget sorrow for sins and hatred of them; next they open to it the beauty of the virtues, and by the example of Christ our Lord kindle it to his imitation. Finally they also hand on a way of reforming one's whole life according to the rule and will of God — whether one's state itself is to be changed, or not changed but corrected for the better.

paras.la: Cum ergo horum exercitiorum tantae sint utilitates tantique fructus, facile apparet, quam eorum usus nostris omnibus commendatus esse debeat — si praesertim illud addamus, quod cum humilitate cognoscere possumus et certe etiam debemus: hoc totum quodcunque est, nempe peculiarem hanc instructionem ac modum meditandi, et peculiaria haec documenta tam utilia tamque solida, esse praeclarum quoddam donum ac munus a Deo datum Societati nostrae. Quare cum id Deus nobis donarit, et ideo donarit ut uteremur, non est dubium quin hoc ipsum excitare omnes debeat, ut avidius utamur, nec talem thesaurum absconditum et quasi defossum inutiliter teneamus.
paras.en: Since, then, the benefits and fruits of these Exercises are so great, it is easy to see how their use ought to be commended to all of ours — especially if we add what we can, and indeed ought, to acknowledge with humility: that this whole thing, whatever it is — this particular instruction and way of meditating, these particular teachings so useful and so solid — is a signal gift and endowment given by God to our Society. Since God has given it to us, and given it that we might use it, there is no doubt that this very fact should stir everyone to use it the more eagerly, and not to keep such a treasure hidden and as it were buried, to no profit.

paras.la: Verum quam utilis est hic exercitiorum usus quem dicimus, tam etiam est necessarium aliquam methodum habere in iis tradendis: tum quia non omnes eandem peritiam aut dexteritatem habere possunt; tum quia non omnia hoc exercitiorum spiritualium libro comprehendi potuerunt, et ideo sunt in eo aliqua paulo obscuriora, quod ad praxim attinet; tum denique etiam, ut servetur a nostris omnibus uniformitas, et non suo quisque ingenio et placito exercitia interpretetur, ex qua re novi ac varii subinde modi introducerentur.
paras.en: But as useful as this practice of the Exercises is, so necessary is it also to have some method in giving them: first, because not everyone can have the same skill or dexterity; next, because not everything could be contained in this book of the Spiritual Exercises, so that some things in it are somewhat obscure as regards practice; and finally, so that uniformity may be kept by all of ours, and each man not interpret the Exercises according to his own bent and pleasure — from which new and divergent ways would time and again be introduced.

paras.rub: Congregationis primae generalis auctoritate Directorium confectum
paras.la: Has igitur ob causas Congregatio prima generalis inter alia, quae necessaria iudicavit ad proximos iuvandos et nostros operarios dirigendos, hoc etiam constituit (tit. 6, decret. 28), ut conficeretur Directorium tradendorum exercitiorum, eiusque rei curam Generali Praeposito commendavit.
paras.en: For these reasons the First General Congregation, among other things it judged necessary for helping our neighbours and directing our workers, also decreed (title 6, decree 28) that a Directory for giving the Exercises should be prepared, and entrusted the care of the matter to the Superior General.

paras.la: In quo cum aliqui Patres diligenter laborassent, vel pro sua devotione, vel Superiorum iussu, visum est P. N. Claudio Acquavivae, tum hunc eorum laborem, tum etiam quae nonnulli alii adumbraverant, quibusdam antiquioribus Patribus in Societate mittere, ut ea viderent, et iudicium de iis ferrent, et praeterea si quid occurreret quod addi posset, in scriptis mandarent. Ex quorum omnium sententiis ac iudiciis ea quae ad nostrum propositum accommodatiora visa sunt, in hoc Directorium selecta et suis locis digesta sunt, ad Dei Domini gloriam, et Societatis nostrae proximorumque spiritualem profectum.
paras.en: When several Fathers had laboured diligently at this — whether out of their own devotion or at the command of superiors — it seemed good to Our Father Claudio Acquaviva to send both their work and the drafts some others had sketched to certain senior Fathers of the Society, that they might examine them, pass judgement on them, and moreover set down in writing anything that occurred to them which might be added. From the opinions and judgements of them all, what seemed best suited to our purpose was selected and arranged in its proper place in this Directory — to the glory of the Lord God, and the spiritual progress of our Society and of our neighbours.

kapitel.label: Cap. I
kapitel.la_titel: Quomodo inducendi sint homines ad Exercitia
kapitel.en_titel: How people are to be led to the Exercises

paras.la: Dicitur in nostris Constitutionibus, cum exercitiorum ratio redditur, non solum id agi debere, ut aliis satisfiat, sed etiam ut in aliis desiderium excitetur, ut eisdem iuvari velint. Ex quo apparet oportere hoc esse nostris propositum, ut quotquot possunt ad agenda exercitia suaviter inducant: quoniam cum charitas et zelus animarum nos movere debeat ad desiderandam et procurandam earum salutem et perfectionem, eadem etiam impellere debet ad eam rem, quae adeo apta et adeo efficax est ad illud utrumque in eis operandum.
paras.en: It is said in our Constitutions, where an account of the Exercises is given, that our aim should be not only to satisfy others, but also to awaken in them the desire to be helped by the Exercises. From this it is plain that our men should make it their purpose gently to lead as many as they can to make the Exercises: for since charity and zeal for souls ought to move us to desire and procure their salvation and perfection, the same charity ought also to impel us toward the thing that is so apt and so effective for working both of these in them.

paras.la: Est tamen opus prudentia, ut id discrete et modeste fiat, nempe tempore et loco convenienti, sine molestia aut offensione, et nominatim cavendo, ne suspicio praebeatur, quod ad religiosum statum trahere velimus. Hunc autem modum prudentem et cautum invitandi ad exercitia suggeret sua cuique prudentia et Spiritus Sancti unctio, quae ut in aliis, ita in hoc diriget et iuvabit suos operarios.
paras.en: Yet prudence is needed, so that this be done discreetly and modestly — at a suitable time and place, without annoyance or offence, and taking particular care that no suspicion be given of wanting to draw anyone toward the religious state. This prudent and careful way of inviting people to the Exercises each man's own prudence will suggest to him, together with the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which in this as in other things will direct and help its workers.

paras.la: Pater noster Ignatius ita sentiebat, et monebat optimum modum esse in confessione, non importune atque ex abrupto, sed aliqua commoda occasione, vel e re nata vel dextre accersita; aut etiam extra confessionem, cum cernitur aliquis non adeo contentus statu suo, sive propter aliquem scrupulum intrinsecum, sive propter molestiam extrinsecam — ut si non bene ei succedant negotia, vel si non bene a suis tractetur, vel ob aliam similem causam. Interdum etiam optima est commoditas ex ipsis vitiis aut lapsibus alicuius, cum praesertim aliquo Dei lumine afflatus ea cognoscit, et dolet, et cupit emendationem. Tunc enim saepe opportunum est proponere ei hoc quasi remedium eius infirmitatis.
paras.en: Our Father Ignatius held, and used to advise, that the best occasion is in confession — not unseasonably or abruptly, but at some convenient opening, whether arising of itself or skilfully brought about; or also outside confession, when one notices that a person is not altogether content with his state, whether from some inward scruple or from some outward trouble — as when his affairs are not going well, or he is not being well treated by his own people, or for some similar reason. Sometimes, too, the best opening is offered by a person's own vices or falls — above all when, touched by some light from God, he recognises them, grieves over them, and desires amendment. Then it is often opportune to propose the Exercises to him as a kind of remedy for his infirmity.

paras.la: Quaecunque vero occasio accipiatur, indicandi sunt magni fructus, qui ex his exercitiis consequi solent: pax et quies animae, lumen interius, et cognitio ad bonam gubernationem totius vitae quocunque in statu.
paras.en: Whatever occasion is taken, the great fruits that usually follow from these Exercises should be pointed out: peace and quiet of soul, inward light, and the knowledge needed for governing one's whole life well in whatever state.

paras.la: Iuvat etiam proponere aliqua exempla aliquorum, qui ea fecerint cum fructu, ita ut postea valde contenti fuerint, ipsaque morum mutatione testati sint quantum in eis profecerint; et ad hoc etiam confert indicare consolationes spirituales et gustus, quos habuerunt — nimirum ne labore deterreantur. Verum in his exemplis commemorandis abstinendum esset ab iis, qui religionem ingressi sunt (vel certe hoc postremum tacendum), et ii potius narrandi, qui in melius mutati in saeculo manserunt: quoniam facile fieri potest, ut quem hortari volumus, idem sibi timeat, et ideo refugiat exercitia.
paras.en: It also helps to set before them examples of persons who have made the Exercises with fruit, so that they were afterwards well content, and by the very change in their conduct bore witness to how much they had profited; and to the same end it is useful to mention the spiritual consolations and relish they experienced — so that the labour may not deter anyone. But in recounting such examples one should refrain from those who entered religion (or at least keep that last point silent), and rather tell of those who, changed for the better, remained in the world: for it can easily happen that the man we wish to encourage fears the same for himself, and therefore shrinks from the Exercises.

paras.la: Immo vero haec ipsa opinio eripienda esset hominibus, ut putent solis religiosis, aut iis qui religiosi fieri volunt, convenire exercitia. Nam cum omnes egeant gratia Dei, non solum religiosi, sed etiam saeculares, propter pericula in quibus assidue vivunt, ideo ipsi quoque debent ea adiumenta quaerere, ex quibus ad hanc gratiam hauriendam quam maxime disponantur.
paras.en: Indeed, this very notion should be taken from people's minds — that the Exercises suit only religious, or those who wish to become religious. For since all stand in need of God's grace, not religious only but seculars as well, on account of the dangers amid which they constantly live, they too ought to seek those helps by which they may be disposed as fully as possible to draw upon that grace.

paras.rub: Qualis mens S. P. N., et quibus danda Exercitia
paras.la: Notandum est tamen, si loquamur de integris et plenis exercitiis, eam fuisse P. Ignatii sententiam, ut non omnibus passim darentur, sed selectis tantum, et qui habiles ad maiora viderentur. Quod ita esse aperte videmus ex quadam instructione, quae conscripta dicitur ipso dictante, quae sic habet: «Non mihi videtur expedire quenquam hortari ad facienda exercitia, nisi has conditiones, vel saltem praecipuas, habeat. Primo, ut eiusmodi sit, qui sperari possit valde utilis futurus domui Dei, si ad eius obsequium vocatus fuerit. Secundo, si nondum habeat eiusmodi talenta iam acquisita artium ac scientiarum, quae hoc praeseferunt, saltem ut eius aetatis atque ingenii sit, ut ad ea aliquando pervenire posse videatur. Tertio, ut liberum sit ei de se ipso statuere, etiam quoad statum perfectionis amplectendum, si Deo placeret eum vocare. Quarto, ut ad spiritualia affectus videatur, habitumque corporis honestum ac decentem habeat. Quinto, ut non ita alicui rei sit addictus, ut ab ea difficulter videatur posse dimoveri, et ad eam aequalitatem perduci, quae requiritur ad hoc negotium animae cum Deo recte tractandum. Ac quanto magis quisque dubius est de vitae suae rationibus, et cupidus sciendi quid facere debeat de sua persona, et denique quanto aptior ad Ecclesiam iuvandam, tanto etiam magis, simpliciter loquendo, idoneus erit ad exercitia facienda. Qui vero has conditiones non haberent, vel qui matrimonio iuncti fuerint, aut alioquin inhabiles, non debent iis tradi exercitia omnia, maxime si alii aptiores ea peterent, vel nostri aliis occupationibus distinerentur. Possent tamen dari eis aliquae meditationes primae hebdomadae, idque si fieri possit, in ipsis eorum domibus, hortando eos, ut in aliqua remotiori domus parte se colligant, unde non nisi ad missam et vesperas egrediantur, aut quando ad meditationes accipiendas veniunt; hisque addi poterunt, si ita videatur, aliqua exercitia, ut triplex modus orandi, et similia.» Haec Pater Ignatius; quae eadem, licet paulo brevius, habentur etiam in Const. p. 7, c. 4, lit. F.
paras.en: It should nevertheless be noted that, if we speak of the entire and complete Exercises, Father Ignatius's judgement was that they should not be given to everyone indiscriminately, but only to select persons who seemed fit for greater things. That this is so we see plainly from a certain instruction said to have been written down at his own dictation, which runs thus: «It does not seem to me expedient to encourage anyone to make the Exercises unless he has these qualifications, or at least the chief of them. First, that he be such that one may hope he will prove very useful to the house of God, should he be called to its service. Second, if he does not yet possess acquired talents in the arts and sciences that give promise of this, that he be at least of such an age and ability that he may be expected to attain them in time. Third, that he be free to decide about himself, even as to embracing the state of perfection, should it please God to call him. Fourth, that he seem drawn to spiritual things, and have a becoming and decent bearing of body. Fifth, that he not be so attached to anything that he seem hard to move from it and to be brought to that equilibrium which is required for treating rightly this business of the soul with God. And the more doubtful a man is about the direction of his life, and the more desirous of knowing what he ought to do with himself, and finally the more apt to help the Church, the more suitable, simply speaking, will he be for making the Exercises. But those who lack these qualifications, or are joined in marriage, or otherwise unsuited, should not be given the Exercises in full — above all if others more apt were asking for them, or our men were taken up with other occupations. Yet some meditations of the First Week could be given to such persons, and this, if it can be done, in their own homes, encouraging them to gather themselves in some more remote part of the house, from which they would go out only for Mass and Vespers, or when they come to receive the meditations; and to these could be added, if it seem good, certain exercises such as the Three Ways of Praying, and the like.» Thus Father Ignatius; and the same points, though somewhat more briefly, are found also in the Constitutions, Part VII, chapter 4, letter F.
paras.note: The inserted instruction is the one the Directory itself attributes to Ignatius's dictation; the Directory quotes it at full length.

kapitel.label: Cap. II
kapitel.la_titel: Quomodo dispositus esse debeat, qui ad exercitia facienda accedit
kapitel.en_titel: How the one who comes to make the Exercises ought to be disposed

paras.la: Qui ad exercitia agenda aggreditur, primo eniti debet, ut intelligat quanta sit res quam aggreditur: nempe quae non solum ad animam pertineat, sed ita pertineat, ut si modo ea diligenter praestet quae debet, iacturus sit fundamenta spiritualis sui profectus, quae deinde tota eius vita usui futura sint. Ex quo intelligat, quantam alacritatem et diligentiam et fortitudinem etiam ad tantum opus tantumque negotium afferre debeat. Itaque statuat ipse secum viriliter agere, et omnia impedimenta divinae gratiae reiicere, et omnes animi sui vires intendere, ut huic gratiae cooperetur, et se ad eam recipiendam quam poterit optime disponat.
paras.en: He who sets about making the Exercises should first strive to understand how great a thing it is he is undertaking: something that concerns not merely his soul, but concerns it in such a way that, if only he performs diligently what he ought, he will be laying the foundations of his spiritual progress, which will serve him for the whole of his life thereafter. From this let him understand how much eagerness, diligence, and even fortitude he ought to bring to so great a work and so great a business. Let him therefore resolve to deal manfully with himself, to cast aside every obstacle to divine grace, and to bend all the powers of his soul to cooperating with that grace and disposing himself as well as he possibly can to receive it.

paras.la: Hanc ob causam ab omnibus aliis negotiis domesticis prius se expediat, vel certe ea aliis interim committat, ac toto tempore omne sibi amicorum ac familiarium, immo etiam nunciorum aut litterarum commercium interdicat: haec enim mentem implere solent variis cogitationibus, quae deinde magnopere distrahunt, et conceptum, si quis est, fervorem restinguunt. Immo vero omnem etiam aliam cogitationem de quavis alia re excludere curet, perinde ac si nullum aliud negotium in hoc mundo haberet.
paras.en: For this reason he should first free himself from all other domestic affairs, or at least commit them to others for the time; and for the whole period he should deny himself all dealings with friends and acquaintances — indeed even with messengers or letters: for these tend to fill the mind with various thoughts, which then greatly distract it and quench whatever fervour has been conceived. Rather, let him take care to shut out every other thought about anything else whatsoever, just as if he had no other business in this world.

paras.la: Habeat deinde magnam spem in Domini bonitate et liberalitate, qui cum etiam errantes requirat et fugientes sequatur, multo magis eos qui ad se bono animo accedunt recipiet et complectetur. Quare confidat in illa infinita clementia, quae cum pium illud desiderium dederit, dabit etiam gratiam ac vires exequendi bene ac fructuose, siquidem eius voluntas est sanctificatio nostra.
paras.en: Next, let him have great hope in the goodness and generosity of the Lord, who — since he seeks out even those who stray and follows after those who flee — will much more receive and embrace those who come to him with good will. Let him therefore trust in that infinite mercy which, having given him that devout desire, will also give the grace and strength to carry it out well and fruitfully — since indeed his will is our sanctification.

paras.la: Inter caetera vero ita etiam animo constitutus esse debet, ut libenter et avide exercitia haec aggrediatur, non tam ut spirituali dulcedine fruatur, quam ut Dei voluntatem de se intelligat, suumque affectum a terrenis omnibus avellat, et eum in suo Creatore collocet. Illud vero maxime necessarium, ut praeter hoc desiderium proficiendi in spiritu sit etiam bene resignatus in beneplacito Dei in iis in quibus adhuc liber est, itaque animo paratus sit, ut quicquid a Deo cognoverit faciendum esse, omnino exequi decreverit.
paras.en: Among other things, he should also be so disposed in mind as to undertake these Exercises willingly and eagerly — not so much to enjoy spiritual sweetness as to understand God's will concerning himself, to tear his affection away from all earthly things, and to set it upon his Creator. And this above all is necessary: that besides this desire of advancing in spirit he be also well resigned to the good pleasure of God in those matters in which he is still free, and so prepared in mind that whatever he comes to know God would have him do, he has resolved to carry out entirely.

paras.la: Quare non debet quisquam deliberationem aliquam secum afferre, a qua dimoveri nolit. Deinde non debet etiam modum ac terminum ipse ponere Dei donis, ita ut usque ad quosdam limites se illuminari ac iuvari velit, non autem amplius. Nam praeterquam quod valde indecens est, ut creatura hoc modo agat cum suo Creatore, valde etiam sibi ipsi nocet: primum quia seipsum privat illis maioribus donis, quae Deus fortasse daturus erat; deinde quia illa ipsa illiberalitas et restrictio et ingratitudo in Deum meretur, ut ne ea quidem accipiat, quae vellet accipere. Quare debet potius animi sinum dilatare, ut quam maxime possit sese cum Deo coniungere, et quam maxime ab eo ditari et locupletari thesauris istis caelestibus desideret. Atque haec quidem observanda sunt ei erga Deum.
paras.en: Therefore no one should bring with him any resolution from which he is unwilling to be moved. Nor, again, should he himself set a measure and limit to God's gifts, wishing to be enlightened and helped only up to certain bounds and no further. For besides its being most unbecoming for a creature to deal in this manner with its Creator, he also does himself great harm: first, because he deprives himself of those greater gifts which God was perhaps going to give; and then because that very illiberality, restriction and ingratitude towards God deserves that he should not receive even what he wished to receive. Rather, he ought to enlarge the bosom of his soul, so that he may unite himself with God as fully as he can, and desire to be enriched and endowed by him to the utmost with those heavenly treasures. So much for what he should observe towards God.

paras.rub: Qualiter se gerat circa dantem Exercitia
paras.la: Erga eum vero qui daturus est exercitia, ita se gerere debet, ut eum accipiat ut magistrum et ducem huius itineris dubii et periculosi; et ideo etiamsi alioqui prudens sit, vel doctus, et in rebus agendis exercitatus, tamen pro hoc tempore non confidat suae prudentiae vel doctrinae, sed totum sese committat huic suo duci, ac quemadmodum ait Apostolus, stultus fiat, ut sit sapiens (1 Cor. 3, 18), illudque Beati Petri monitum exequatur: sicut modo geniti infantes... sine dolo lac concupiscite, ut in eo crescatis in salutem (1 Petr. 2, 2). Itaque instructorem suum ita intueatur, tanquam Dei instrumentum ad hoc sibi missum, ut eum dirigat et perducat per eam viam quae ad vitam ducit. Quam ob causam cum omni reverentia et alacritate et confidentia excipere debebit quae ei proponet.
paras.en: Towards the one who is to give him the Exercises he should so conduct himself as to receive him as the master and guide of this uncertain and perilous journey. Therefore, even if he is otherwise prudent, or learned, and practised in the conduct of affairs, for this time he should not rely on his own prudence or learning, but commit himself wholly to this guide of his and, as the Apostle says, become a fool that he may be wise (1 Cor 3:18), and carry out that counsel of blessed Peter: like newborn infants, desire the guileless milk, that by it you may grow unto salvation (1 Pet 2:2). Let him look upon his instructor as an instrument of God sent to him for this purpose — to direct him and lead him along the way that leads to life. For this reason he ought to receive with all reverence, readiness and confidence whatever the instructor sets before him.

paras.la: Praeterea nihil eum celet, nihil dissimulet, sed sincere totum cor suum ei patefaciat, et candide referat quomodo singulae meditationes successerint, quas in eis vel extra eas reliquo tempore consolationes, desolationes, lumina vel bona desideria senserit. Denique obediat ei in omnibus perfecte, neque alias meditationes aut alium ordinem teneat quam ille praescripserit, idemque in poenitentiis et corporis castigationibus; et in summa hoc sibi persuadeat: quo diligentius et exactius illius ductum sequetur, eo aptiorem fore ad Dei gratiam largius accipiendam, quia illa humilitas et illa simplicitas valde Deo placet, et cum talibus est eius sermocinatio. Haec igitur necessaria quidem sunt, ut plenior fructus eliciatur.
paras.en: Furthermore, let him hide nothing from him and dissemble nothing, but sincerely lay open to him his whole heart, and candidly report how each meditation has gone — what consolations, desolations, lights or good desires he has felt in them or outside them during the rest of the time. Finally, let him obey him perfectly in everything, and keep to no other meditations and no other order than he has prescribed, and likewise in penances and bodily austerities. In sum, let him persuade himself of this: the more diligently and exactly he follows his guidance, the more apt he will be to receive God's grace in fuller measure — for such humility and such simplicity please God greatly, and with such souls is his conversation. These things, then, are necessary if the fuller fruit is to be drawn out.

paras.la: Sed tamen si is qui tradit exercitia timeret, ne si omnia proponat exercitia facturo, fortasse eum deterreant ac retrahant, melius esset vel aliqua tantum horum proponere ab initio, vel non admodum exaggerare; sed si postea cum gustu spirituali eum affici viderit, magisque capacem ad haec portanda, tunc eum paulatim excitare ad exercitia peragenda cum omni perfectione.
paras.en: If, however, the one giving the Exercises should fear that setting all of this before the future exercitant might perhaps deter and hold him back, it would be better either to propose only some of these things at the outset, or not to press them too strongly; and then, if he later sees him touched with spiritual relish and more capable of bearing these demands, gradually to rouse him to carry the Exercises through with all perfection.

kapitel.label: Cap. III
kapitel.la_titel: De quibus monendus sit Exercitia ingrediens, et de tempore meditandi
kapitel.en_titel: What the one entering the Exercises is to be advised of, and on the time for meditation

paras.la: Sunt etiam alia, de quibus monendus est qui facit exercitia; sed quia haec continentur in annotationibus vel regulis scriptis in libro exercitiorum, non est quod hic repetantur. Hoc tamen de iis addendum: debere eum omnem diligentiam ponere in eis observandis, quoniam quo diligentior in hoc fuerit, eo citius et uberius inveniet fructum spiritualem qui quaeritur.
paras.en: There are other points too of which the one making the Exercises should be advised; but since these are contained in the Annotations, or in the rules written in the book of the Exercises, there is no need to repeat them here. This much, however, should be added: he ought to put all diligence into observing them, for the more diligent he is in this, the more quickly and abundantly he will find the spiritual fruit that is sought.

paras.la: Illud etiam in particulari attingi potest: non debere eum legere nisi scripta quae ei traduntur, nec libros habere in cubiculo, ut occasio legendi praecidatur — praeter Breviarium, si sacerdos sit, aut Officium Beatae Virginis. Si tamen instructori videbitur, posset in prima hebdomada legere librum Gersonis de imitatione Christi, in secunda aliquid ex Evangeliis et Sanctorum vita, ut dicitur in annotationibus post primam meditationem secundae hebdomadae. Sed has vitas sanctorum oporteret esse selectas, et valde accommodatas ei qui facit exercitia: ut si esset uxoratus, oporteret ei tradere vitam alicuius qui sancte vixisset in saeculo; similiter in religiosis, et in aliis similibus. Quare is labor et diligentia esse deberet instructoris in idoneis seligendis.
paras.en: One particular may also be touched on: he should read nothing except the papers given to him, and should keep no books in his room, so that the occasion for reading is cut off — apart from the Breviary, if he is a priest, or the Office of Our Lady. If, however, it seems good to the instructor, he might in the First Week read Gerson's book on the Imitation of Christ, and in the Second something from the Gospels and from the lives of the saints, as is said in the annotations after the first meditation of the Second Week. But these lives of the saints would need to be select, and well suited to the one making the Exercises: if he were a married man, he should be given the life of someone who lived holily in the world; likewise for religious, and in other similar cases. Here, then, the instructor's labour and diligence should go into choosing what is suitable.

paras.la: Porro in Evangeliis non debet legere nisi illud mysterium, quod eadem hora vel die est meditaturus, ut habetur in primo notabili post quintam contemplationem secundae hebdomadae.
paras.en: Further, in the Gospels he should read only that mystery which he is to meditate at that same hour or on that same day, as is laid down in the first note after the fifth contemplation of the Second Week.

paras.la: Tamen si post factam meditationem taedio affici videretur, ac potius tempus perdere, posset etiam, ut dictum est, addi aliquis alius liber: ut prima hebdomada Dionysius Carthusianus de quatuor novissimis, Confessiones sancti Augustini, aut similes — hoc advertendo, ut non solum boni et utiles sint, verum etiam apti et opportuni ad gignendum illum affectum, qui eo tempore in exercitiis quaeritur, ut contritionem, vel timorem, vel Dei amorem. Quinetiam monendus est et docendus, ut ipsam lectionem dirigat ad meditationem: nimirum non legendo cursim aviditate sciendi et videndi nova, sed immorando, et perpendendo accurate ea quae legit, et intrando in eosdem affectus.
paras.en: If, however, after making his meditation he should seem to be overcome by weariness and rather to be losing time, some other book might also, as has been said, be added: in the First Week, Denis the Carthusian on the Four Last Things, the Confessions of Saint Augustine, or the like — with this proviso, that the books be not only good and useful, but also apt and well-timed for begetting the affection that is sought at that stage of the Exercises, such as contrition, or fear, or the love of God. Moreover, he should be advised and taught to direct the reading itself toward meditation: that is, not reading cursorily out of eagerness to know and to see new things, but dwelling on what he reads, weighing it carefully, and entering into the same affections.

paras.la: Quod de legendo dicitur, idem de scribendo dicendum. Nihil enim aliud scribi debet praeter ea quae pertinent ad orationem: nempe puncta aliqua quae Dominus communicaverit in meditatione, vel etiam extra meditationem — quae tamen brevissime notanda sunt, non diffuse per modum sermonis. Haec autem puncta possunt esse duplicis generis: vel practica, quae pertinent ad agendum, ut sunt desideria quaedam, aut firmae deliberationes faciendi aliquid; vel quae pertinent ad cognoscendum, ut sunt quaedam veritates aut lumina circa aliquam materiam — ut alicuius virtutis, v. g. humilitatis, contemptus mundi, patientiae etc., vel etiam in aliqua materia meditationis, ut incarnationis vel passionis Domini — et similia eiusmodi, praesertim quae sint quasi axiomata quaedam, et viam aperiant ad bene percipiendas ac meditandas illas materias.
paras.en: What is said of reading applies equally to writing. Nothing should be written down except what pertains to prayer: namely certain points which the Lord has communicated in meditation, or even outside meditation — and these should be noted very briefly, not at length in the manner of a discourse. Such points can be of two kinds: either practical, pertaining to action, such as certain desires, or firm resolutions to do something; or pertaining to knowledge, such as certain truths or lights concerning some matter — some virtue, for example humility, contempt of the world, patience, and so on, or some matter of meditation, such as the Incarnation or the Passion of the Lord — and other things of this sort, above all such as are like axioms, opening the way to perceiving and meditating those matters well.

paras.la: Sed illud cavendum, ne vel legendi vel scribendi dulcedine ita se quispiam distineri sinat, ut tempus eripiatur meditationi, aut etiam praeparationi ad meditationem. Semper enim aliquanto ante meditationem debet omnia relinquere, et omnino suam cogitationem convertere ad puncta illius exercitii quod iam instat. Addo etiam, cavendum hoc quoque, ne nimis legendo aut scribendo defatigetur animus, et quasi vires eius exhauriantur: oportet enim salvam semper relinqui meditationem, et caetera omnia huic uni servire.
paras.en: But care must be taken that no one lets himself be so held by the sweetness of reading or of writing that time is stolen from the meditation, or even from the preparation for it. He should always, a little while before the meditation, leave everything aside and turn his thought entirely to the points of the exercise now at hand. I add that care must also be taken that the mind not be worn out by too much reading or writing, its powers as it were drained: the meditation must always be kept intact, and everything else made to serve this one thing.

paras.la: Qui exercitia exacte facere volunt viresque idoneas habent, iis quinque horae meditandi quotidie praescribi solent: prima circa mediam noctem, quod tempus propter quietem ac profundum silentium valde aptum est meditationi; secunda sub auroram; tertia paulo ante prandium; quarta post meridiem; quinta sub vesperam. Et post uniuscuiusque horae meditationem quadrans etiam ad examen praecedentis meditationis.
paras.en: For those who wish to make the Exercises exactly and have the requisite strength, five hours of meditation a day are customarily prescribed: the first about midnight — a time which, for its quiet and deep silence, is very apt for meditation; the second toward dawn; the third shortly before dinner; the fourth after midday; the fifth toward evening. And after the meditation of each hour, a quarter-hour besides for the examination of the meditation just made.

paras.la: Cum aliis, qui debilioris sunt valetudinis, vel tam exactum modum servare non possunt, dispensari poterit de hora mediae noctis, ita tamen ut quinque horae maneant, aut etiam pauciores, si instructor ita expedire iudicaverit. Ut vero plures sint quam quinque, raro continget ut expediat: nam cum nimis continuantur haec exercitia mentis, ita retundi solet, ut obtusior etiam reddatur intellectus, et voluntas minus efficax.
paras.en: With others, who are of weaker health or cannot keep so exact a measure, a dispensation may be given from the midnight hour — yet so that five hours remain, or even fewer, if the instructor judges it expedient. That there should be more than five will rarely prove expedient: for when these exercises of the mind are continued too long, the mind is so blunted that the understanding becomes duller and the will less effective.

kapitel.label: Cap. IV
kapitel.la_titel: De loco exercitiis idoneo, et de quibusdam particularibus
kapitel.en_titel: On a place suited to the Exercises, and on certain particulars

paras.la: Locus ad facienda exercitia non est dubium, quin debeat esse remotus ab hominum concursu et aspectu, etiam maxime familiarium. Ita enim monet Pater N. Ignatius annotatione ultima, ubi etiam tres eius rei commemorat utilitates. Quare si exercitia suscepturus alibi tam commode et tam fructuose non potest, et Superiori ita videatur, poterit excipi domi nostrae — sed in aliquo cubiculo, quod sit quam maxime separatum ab aliis cubiculis et officinis domesticis, ut quam minime videat vel audiat quae a nostris fiunt.
paras.en: As for the place for making the Exercises, there is no doubt that it ought to be removed from the concourse and sight of men — above all of one's own household and friends. So Our Father Ignatius advises in the last Annotation, where he also recounts three advantages of this. Hence, if the one about to make the Exercises cannot do so as conveniently and fruitfully elsewhere, and the Superior thinks fit, he may be received in our own house — but in a room as far separated as possible from the other rooms and the working quarters of the house, so that he may see or hear as little as possible of what our men do.

paras.la: Quod vero ad expensas attinet, cum ille in domum nostram venerit, consulatur superior: ad cuius prudentiam pertinebit ita omnia moderari, ut neque domus nimium gravetur, neque contra, occasione domus non gravandae, minuatur numerus eorum qui exercitia facere possunt. Videntur autem communiter nec recusandae, si offerantur, praesertim a ditioribus, nec, si non offerantur, requirendae. Absit vero semper quicquid in eo genere sordidum aut indecorum videri possit.
paras.en: As to expenses, when such a one comes to our house, the superior should be consulted; it will belong to his prudence so to regulate everything that the house is not too much burdened, nor, on the other hand, the number of those able to make the Exercises reduced for the sake of sparing the house. As a general rule it seems that payment should neither be refused if offered — especially by the wealthier — nor demanded if not offered. But let anything that could appear sordid or unseemly in this matter be always far away.

paras.la: In hoc loco praeter instructorem debet etiam esse qui inserviat, et necessaria ad victum deferat. Hunc autem oportet esse fidelem, discretum, taciturnum, quique sua modestia et humilitatis ac devotionis exemplo aedificet. Nihil autem loquetur, nisi de iis quae ad victum aut cubiculum et ministerium suum pertineant, idque paucissimis, omnia semper ad instructorem reiiciendo; quem etiam de singulis certiorem faciet, nec rem ullam ei deferet, etiam postulatus, nisi illo consulto.
paras.en: In this place, besides the instructor, there should also be someone to serve the exercitant and bring him what he needs for his meals. This man ought to be faithful, discreet, silent, and such as edifies by his modesty and by his example of humility and devotion. He is to say nothing except about what concerns the food, the room, and his own service, and that in the fewest words, always referring everything to the instructor; he will also keep the instructor informed of every detail, and will bring the exercitant nothing, even if asked, without consulting him.
paras.note: The heading's 'exercitanti' — 'the exercitant' — is the Directory's usual term for the one making the Exercises.

paras.la: Componet lectum, et cubiculum verret opportuno tempore, quod fere erit tempore missae. Caetera etiam, quae opus erit, munda et apta afferet, praeseferendo semper magnam charitatem et diligentiam; atque inter alia meminerit etiam pro ipso orare quotidie.
paras.en: He will make the bed and sweep the room at a convenient time, which will usually be during Mass. Whatever else is needed he will bring clean and in good order, always showing great charity and diligence; and among other things let him remember also to pray for the exercitant daily.

paras.la: Aliquando etiam profuit huic ministerio eum deputare, qui notus aut familiaris esset exercitanti; idque iuvat non solum ad consolationem quandam ipsius, sed etiam ad profectum spiritualem, quoniam aliqui interdum confidentius se aperiunt amicis huiusmodi quam ipsi instructori, si eum nunquam antea norant. Sed hoc totum pendere debet ex iudicio eius qui tradit exercitia, ut videat quatenus hic progredi debeat, quid loqui, et quomodo. Debet enim uti eo tamquam instrumento suo, iuxta id quod intelliget convenire ad maiorem utilitatem exercitantis.
paras.en: Sometimes it has also proved profitable to assign to this service someone known to or friendly with the exercitant; this helps not only toward a certain consolation for him, but also toward his spiritual progress, since some people at times open themselves more confidently to such friends than to the instructor himself, if they have never known him before. But all of this must depend on the judgement of the one giving the Exercises, who should determine how far this man may go, what he may say, and in what manner: for he ought to use him as his own instrument, according to what he understands to serve the greater benefit of the exercitant.

paras.la: Quod ad victum attinet, quaerendum est ab eo, quid sibi parari velit, idque ei afferendum, quod ille petierit.
paras.en: As for food, he should be asked what he would like prepared for him, and what he asks for should be brought to him.

paras.la: Praeter hunc qui ei ministrat, ut plurimum non debet ab aliis visitari. Nam de saecularibus quidem nulla est dubitatio, nisi aliqua necessitas urgeret. Ex nostris autem aliquis mitti posset, cum vel qui facit exercitia id peteret ab instructore, vel instructor, etiam illo non petente, ita iudicaret ad eius consolationem vel profectum.
paras.en: Apart from the one who serves him, he should as a rule not be visited by others. About seculars, indeed, there is no question — unless some necessity urged. But one of our men might be sent, either when the one making the Exercises asks this of the instructor, or when the instructor, even unasked, judges it to be for his consolation or progress.

paras.la: Quicumque autem eat, cavere debet ut nullus nisi utilis sermo habeatur, ac de rebus spiritualibus — nulla tamen significatione quod eum ad hunc vel illum vitae statum impellere velit, praesertim vero ad Societatem. Nam praeterquam quod vocatio debet esse libera et a Deo venire, ipsi etiam qui in hac deliberatione versantur, si id intelligant aut suspicentur, eo magis retrahi solent; et contra, ut experientia saepe ostendit, eo magis incitari, cum in nostris nullam talem cupiditatem animadvertunt.
paras.en: Whoever goes, however, must take care that no conversation be held except what is useful, and about spiritual things — yet with no hint of wishing to push him toward this or that state of life, and least of all toward the Society. For besides the fact that a vocation must be free and come from God, those who are engaged in this deliberation, if they perceive or suspect such a design, usually draw back all the more; and on the contrary, as experience has often shown, they are the more drawn on when they notice in our men no such eagerness.

kapitel.label: Cap. V
kapitel.la_titel: Qualis esse, et quid facere debeat qui exercitia tradit
kapitel.en_titel: What sort of man he ought to be who gives the Exercises, and what he ought to do

paras.la: Quod ad illum attinet, qui exercitia traditurus est, illud primum a P. N. Ignatio 4. parte, cap. 8, § 5 praecipitur, ut prius ea in se ipso sit expertus, ut rationem eorum reddere possit, et dexteritatem in iis tradendis habere. Quod ut facilius assequatur (ut ibidem dicitur in declaratione), prius quibusdam tradere deberet, in quibus minor esset iactura, si quid erretur — ut, verbi gratia, iunioribus, aut iis qui non ingressuri sunt electionem de vitae statu. Deinde etiam proderit conferre suum modum procedendi cum aliquo magis exercitato, bene adnotando quid magis vel minus convenire deprehenderit. Itaque hoc primum et praecipuum esse debet: ut sit bene versatus in rebus spiritualibus, et nominatim in his exercitiis.
paras.en: As regards the one who is to give the Exercises, the first precept, from Our Father Ignatius in Part IV, chapter 8, § 5, is that he should first have experienced them in himself, so that he can give an account of them and have skill in giving them. To attain this more easily (as is said in the declaration in the same place), he should first give them to persons with whom less would be lost if some mistake were made — for example, to younger men, or to those who are not going to enter upon an election of a state of life. It will also profit him to compare his manner of proceeding with someone more practised, noting well what he finds to answer better or worse. So this must be the first and chief requirement: that he be well versed in spiritual things, and in these Exercises in particular.

paras.la: Praeterea sit prudens et discretus, parcus et moderatus, consideratus in sermone. Sit etiam suavis potius quam austerus, maxime cum iis qui tentationes, vel etiam desolationes, aut ariditates et taedia patiuntur: quos consolari, animare et erigere debet opportunis consiliis, et precibus tum suis, tum aliorum. Expedit etiam ut gratus ei sit qui facit exercitia, quoniam hoc modo magis ei confidet, seque magis aperiet.
paras.en: Further, let him be prudent and discreet, sparing and moderate, considered in speech. Let him also be gentle rather than austere — above all with those who suffer temptations, or desolations, dryness and weariness; these he ought to console, encourage and lift up with timely counsels, and with prayers both his own and others'. It is also expedient that he be pleasing to the one making the Exercises, since in this way the latter will trust him more, and open himself more.

paras.la: Porro in agendo cum ipso meminerit auctoritatem quandam semper retinere, servata quadam maturitate et gravitate — eoque etiam magis, quo is qui in exercitiis versatur maior ipse fuerit. Hoc enim valde expedit ad eius spiritualem profectum, ut locum et personam magistri, ut vere est, tueatur. Etsi haec auctoritas temperata esse debet humilitate religiosa, quae eluceat in omnibus eius dictis et factis, ita ut ne vestigium quidem ullius vanitatis conspiciatur; sed in hoc Christum imitari debet, qui cum forma esset omnis modestiae, tamen, sicut scriptum est, loquebatur tamquam potestatem habens (Matt. 7, 29; Marc. 1, 22). Itaque cum omni libertate officium suum exequi debebit — tum docendo, tum monendo, tum dirigendo, ubi quippiam curvum aut distortum esse viderit.
paras.en: Moreover, in dealing with the exercitant let him remember always to retain a certain authority, keeping a certain maturity and gravity — and the more so, the greater the person making the Exercises. For it greatly serves the exercitant's spiritual progress that the instructor maintain the place and person of a master, as he truly is. Yet this authority must be tempered with religious humility, shining out in all his words and deeds, so that not even a trace of any vanity be seen; herein he should imitate Christ, who, though he was the very pattern of all modesty, nevertheless, as it is written, spoke as one having authority (Mt 7:29; Mk 1:22). And so he should carry out his office with entire freedom — teaching, admonishing, and setting straight whatever he sees to be crooked or distorted.

paras.la: Caveat, cum bonum aliquem effectum viderit in iis qui se exercent, quicquam suae industriae aut peritiae tribuere: cum hi omnes effectus gratiae sint a solo Deo, et consilia extrinsecus adhibita — praeterquam quod, si bona sunt, ab eodem Deo sunt — tantam vim habeant, et tantum operentur, quantum concurrit et cooperatur Deus. Ex altera tamen parte multum confidat in Domino, et ab eo speret certum auxilium tum sibi, tum ei qui facit exercitia.
paras.en: When he sees some good effect in those who are making the Exercises, let him beware of ascribing anything to his own industry or skill: all these effects of grace are from God alone, and the counsels applied from without — besides the fact that, if they are good, they too are from the same God — have only as much force and accomplish only as much as God concurs and cooperates. Yet on the other side let him trust much in the Lord, and hope from him sure help both for himself and for the one making the Exercises.

paras.rub: Sinat Deum de sua creatura disponere
paras.la: Illud autem valde observandum: ut nihil de suo apponat; sed cum eiusmodi consilia debeant ex divina inspiratione suscipi, caveat ne indiscreto zelo conetur aliquid ei suadere, sed sinat Deum de sua creatura disponere iuxta placitum bonitatis suae. Quod ut melius et facilius in opere praestet, servet se in animo plane indifferentem, et in nihil aliud eius voluntas feratur, nisi ut sanctissimum Dei beneplacitum in anima illa plene et perfecte compleatur; et ipse tantum in eo laboret, ut qui se exercet id investigare sciat, et sciat se a daemonis deceptionibus expedire, quibus homines retardare solet.
paras.en: This above all must be observed: that he add nothing of his own. Since counsels of this kind ought to be received from divine inspiration, let him beware of trying, with indiscreet zeal, to persuade the exercitant to anything; rather let him allow God to dispose of his own creature according to the good pleasure of his goodness. That he may accomplish this better and more easily in practice, let him keep himself in mind entirely indifferent, and let his will be carried toward nothing else than that the most holy good pleasure of God be fully and perfectly accomplished in that soul; and let his own labour go only to this — that the one exercising himself may know how to search that will out, and know how to free himself from the deceptions of the demon, with which he is wont to hold men back.
paras.note: This paragraph condenses the Fifteenth Annotation of the Exercises, which the margin of the print cites.

paras.la: Curet etiam perspectum habere eum qui facit exercitia, non tantum quoad statum et conditionem — si nobilis sit vel plebeius, doctus vel indoctus etc. — sed etiam quoad peculiares quasdam partes: ut si simplex vel prudens sit, si provectus in rebus spiritualibus, an adhuc rudis ac novus, si intelligens et capax, an vero hebetior et tardior. Nam cum diversis diverso modo agendum est: ut rudioribus sunt res explicatius proponendae, aliis autem brevius etc.
paras.en: Let him also take care to know well the one making the Exercises — not only as to his state and condition, whether noble or common, learned or unlearned, and so forth, but also as to certain particular traits: whether he is simple or shrewd, advanced in spiritual things or still raw and new, intelligent and capable, or rather dull and slow. For different persons must be dealt with in different ways: to the less practised things must be set out more fully, to others more briefly, and so on.

paras.la: Illud autem in primis necessarium, ut qui exercitia traditurus est totum librum exercitiorum perlegerit, eumque prae manibus habeat, et praesertim annotationes et regulas. Neque sufficit cursim ea videre, sed omnia accurate, immo singulas pene voces expendere oportet: quoniam quaedam sunt in iis brevissime dicta, quae magnum pondus habent, et ignorata aut praeterita damnum afferunt. Itaque tum antea accurate ea vidisse oportebit, tum vero in dandis exercitiis relegenda erunt accuratius, praesertim quae pertinent ad illud tempus, in quo tum versatur ille qui suscipit.
paras.en: This is necessary above all: that he who is to give the Exercises should have read through the whole book of the Exercises and have it at hand — especially the Annotations and the Rules. Nor is it enough to glance through them: everything must be weighed with care, indeed almost every single word, for some things are said there most briefly which carry great weight, and which, if unknown or passed over, do harm. So he will need both to have studied them carefully beforehand, and, while giving the Exercises, to reread more carefully those parts especially which bear on the stage at which the one receiving them then stands.

paras.la: Iuvabit etiam ut singula exercitia, antequam ea tradat, aliquantulum ipse meditetur, si fieri poterit, ut melius imprimat alteri.
paras.en: It will help, too, if before giving each exercise he himself meditates it a little, where that can be done, so as to impress it the better on the other.

kapitel.label: Cap. VI
kapitel.la_titel: De visitando eo qui exercetur
kapitel.en_titel: On visiting the one who is making the Exercises

paras.la: Coeptis exercitiis, sit diligens in visitando suis temporibus eo qui exercetur. Videtur autem expedire, ut quotidie semel eum adeat, neque tamen saepius, nisi aliqua occurreret necessitas — ut aliquando accidit prima hebdomada propter rei novitatem, aut secunda propter difficultatem electionis.
paras.en: Once the Exercises have begun, let the instructor be diligent in visiting the exercitant at the proper times. It seems expedient that he go to him once a day, but not more often, unless some necessity should arise — as sometimes happens in the First Week because of the newness of the thing, or in the Second because of the difficulty of the election.

paras.la: Immo cum aliquibus hominibus gravibus, et bene introductis in spiritu et devotione, posset etiam aliquando esse utilius ut aliquis dies omitteretur. De tempore autem eum visitandi, videat ipse quod sit commodius et aptius. Ex natura quidem sua videtur matutinum, quia tunc animus est magis dispositus ad res percipiendas et penetrandas. Quamquam sub vesperam solet esse maior necessitas, quia tunc interdum magis crescunt tentationes et desolationes, quia animus est minus aptus ad contemplandum, et ideo interdum incidit in morositatem quandam, et magis est expositus tentationibus.
paras.en: Indeed, with certain grave persons, well grounded in spirit and devotion, it might sometimes even be more useful to let a day pass. As for the time of visiting him, let the instructor himself see what is more convenient and fitting. Of its nature the morning seems best, because then the mind is better disposed to grasp and penetrate things. Yet toward evening the need is often greater, because then temptations and desolations sometimes grow stronger, the mind being less apt for contemplation, so that at times it falls into a certain moroseness and is more exposed to temptations.

paras.la: Videat etiam instructor, an aliquando ex peculiari causa expediat, ut statim a prandio vel a caena ipse, vel aliquis alius maturus et discretus ab eo designandus, cum eo qui est in exercitiis maneat ad honestam recreationem.
paras.en: Let the instructor also consider whether at times, for some particular reason, it may be expedient that immediately after dinner or supper he himself — or some other mature and discreet man appointed by him — remain with the one in the Exercises for honest recreation.

kapitel.label: Cap. VII
kapitel.la_titel: De exigenda ratione meditationis
kapitel.en_titel: On requiring an account of the meditation

paras.la: Igitur, quodcunque tempus elegerit ad eum invisendum, cum ad ipsum venerit, interrogabit quomodo se habuerit ab ea hora qua illum postremo vidit, et praesertim in meditatione: nimirum quem modum tenuit in meditando, quos mentis discursus, quas voluntatis motiones habuerit, quas consolationes senserit, et in quibus punctis.
paras.en: Whatever time, then, he has chosen for visiting him, when he comes to him he will ask how he has fared since the hour he last saw him, and especially in the meditation: namely, what method he kept in meditating, what reasonings of the mind and what movements of the will he has had, what consolations he has felt, and at which points.

paras.la: Si bene procedit et consolationibus abundat, non illum laudare oportet, ne sibi complaceat; sed primum doceat quomodo solidum fructum ex illis consolationibus elicere debeat. Nam si nihil aliud fiat, abeunte illo suavi sensu, qui fere non diu durare solet, nullus fructus remaneret. Quare instruendus est ut eas consolationes dirigat ad morum emendationem vitaeque totius institutionem, quia, ut scriptum est, non auditores legis, sed factores iustificantur (Rom. 2, 13). Atque hic etiam monendus est, ut breviter in scripto ponat notabiliores consolationes et lumina, desideria quoque et firmas deliberationes faciendi aliquid: quoniam proderunt multum alio tempore, cum ea non habebit.
paras.en: If he is going on well and abounds in consolations, one ought not to praise him, lest he grow pleased with himself; rather let the instructor first teach him how to draw solid fruit from those consolations. For if nothing more is done, once that sweet feeling departs — and it rarely lasts long — no fruit would remain. He should therefore be instructed to direct those consolations toward the amendment of his conduct and the ordering of his whole life, since, as it is written, not the hearers of the law but the doers are justified (Rom 2:13). And here he should also be advised to set down briefly in writing the more notable consolations and lights, along with desires and firm resolutions to do something: for they will profit him much at another time, when he no longer has them.

paras.la: Deinde vero praeparet illum ad tempus desolationis et ariditatis, quae solent frequenter contingere, ne deinde, cum contigerit, imparatus sit. Atque hoc tempore, cum res bene succedit, non oportet diu cum ipso remanere, sed sinendum ut Creator cum creatura sua, et haec vicissim cum illo transigat — nisi necessarium videretur ad eum vel dirigendum, vel etiam recreandum, si nimis absorptus esset cogitationibus illis.
paras.en: Next let him prepare him for the time of desolation and dryness, which are wont to come frequently, so that when they come he may not be caught unprepared. And at this time, while things are going well, there is no need to stay long with him: the Creator should be allowed to deal with his creature, and the creature in turn with him — unless it should seem necessary either to direct him, or even to give him relief, if he were too much absorbed in those thoughts.

paras.la: Contra vero, si exercitans aridus sit et desolatus, aut distractus in meditando, percunctari debet quomodo se gesserit in meditatione, et nominatim quomodo observarit additiones; et si in aliqua remissum invenerit, moneat et instruat.
paras.en: On the contrary, if the exercitant is dry and desolate, or distracted in his meditation, the instructor should inquire how he conducted himself in the meditation, and in particular how he observed the Additions; and if he finds him slack in any of them, let him admonish and instruct him.

paras.la: Aperiat etiam ei viam ad meditationem, attingendo et quasi indicando aliquos conceptus, quos deinde ipse cogitatione prosequatur.
paras.en: Let him also open for him a way into the meditation, touching on and as it were pointing out certain thoughts, which the exercitant may then pursue in his own reflection.

paras.la: Hortetur ad patientiam et longanimitatem, ne se obrui sinat taedio, ac propter molestiam et laborem avertatur ab oratione: quia si fortiter cum spe ac fiducia perseveret pulsare ad ostium misericordiae divinae, non poterit non aperire, iuxta illud: Si moram fecerit, expecta eum, quia veniet, et non tardabit (Habac. 2, 3).
paras.en: Let him exhort him to patience and long-suffering, not to let himself be overwhelmed by weariness, nor to be turned away from prayer by its trouble and labour: for if he perseveres bravely, with hope and confidence, in knocking at the door of the divine mercy, it cannot fail to open, according to the word: If he delays, wait for him, for he will surely come, and will not be late (Hab 2:3).

paras.la: Moneat etiam optimum remedium consequendi a Deo devotionem esse, ut humilietur sub potenti manu Dei, et se subiiciat ac resignet eius divinae voluntati. Saepe enim illa displicentia et amaritudo non tam venit ex fervore, quam ex tacita quadam superbia, qua homo confidit in sua diligentia, vel quia in eo etiam vellet excellere, aut ex amore proprio, quia amat consolationem. Quare hoc omnino observandum est: ut cum fecerit quod in se est, caetera permittat divinae voluntati et charitati, et confidat quod illa ipsa ariditas ideo permittitur a Deo, quia sibi sic expedit. Et hic ipse affectus humilitatis et subiectionis erga Deum saepe magis efficax est, ut concedat gratiam bene orandi.
paras.en: Let him advise him too that the best remedy for obtaining devotion from God is to humble himself under God's mighty hand, and to submit and resign himself to his divine will. For that displeasure and bitterness often come not so much from fervour as from a certain hidden pride, by which a man trusts in his own diligence, or would even wish to excel in this too; or from self-love, because he loves consolation. Therefore this must be observed absolutely: having done what lies in him, let him leave the rest to the divine will and charity, and trust that this very dryness is permitted by God because it is thus expedient for him. And this very disposition of humility and submission toward God is often more effective in winning the grace of praying well.

paras.la: In primis autem caveat instructor, ne unquam det ei occasionem suspicandi, quod minus bonam opinionem de se habeat, etiam si non ita se bene gesserit; sed ostendat illi semper se bene sperare, et sua spe etiam illi animum ac spem addat.
paras.en: Above all, let the instructor beware of ever giving him occasion to suspect that he holds a poorer opinion of him — even if he has not conducted himself so well; rather let him always show that he hopes well of him, and by his own hope give him too courage and hope.

kapitel.label: Cap. VIII
kapitel.la_titel: De proponenda meditatione
kapitel.en_titel: On proposing the meditation

paras.la: In proponendis punctis meditationum non oportebit ea valde exaggerare, aut etiam ita enucleare, ut qui meditatur ipse nihil novi per se invenire possit, aut certe aegre. Experientia enim docet magis omnes delectari et moveri etiam iis quae per se inveniunt; et ideo satis erit quasi digito indicare venam, quam deinde sibi quisque effodiat. Si tamen essent aliqui parum capaces, iis possent paulo magis declarari.
paras.en: In proposing the points of the meditations it will not be necessary to elaborate them at length, nor to shell them out so completely that the one meditating can find nothing new for himself, or only with difficulty. Experience teaches that everyone takes more delight, and is more moved, by what he discovers for himself; and so it will suffice, as it were, to point out the vein with a finger, and let each then dig it out for himself. Yet if some were of small capacity, the points might be explained to them a little more fully.
paras.note: The margin cites the Second Annotation, which this paragraph restates.

paras.la: Ipsae autem meditationes dari solent in scriptis, ne fatigetur memoria exercitantis, quod solet impedire devotionem, cum vires omnes sint integrae reservandae intellectui et voluntati.
paras.en: The meditations themselves are usually given in writing, so that the exercitant's memory be not wearied — a thing which tends to hinder devotion, since all his powers should be kept whole for the understanding and the will.

paras.la: Denique inter alia quae instructor attendere debet, est etiam illud: ne qui exercetur caput laedat nimia attentione orandi. Est enim magnum huius periculum, tum tempore desolationis, quo anima magis conniti solet, quasi adverso flumine, tum etiam consolationis, cum se totam dat propitiis ventis. Quare non sufficit monere de moderatione servanda: nam cum ii qui exercitia faciunt ut plurimum sint rudes et novi in meditando, non ita possunt cognoscere quid sibi nociturum est; sed oportet interrogare quem modum servent in elevanda mente in Deum et in ea retinenda in Deo, et nominatim in compositione loci. Ac si appareat eos sibi vim facere, docendi sunt de modo ac ratione cogitandi suaviter de divinis: primo, quia alioquin durari non potest, et impeditur meditatio; deinde etiam quia solidus fructus consistit in cognitione illarum veritatum et voluntatis motione, quae procedunt ex lumine intimo — non autem in hac attentione violenta, aut in coactitiis illis lachrymis, quas merito irridet Cassianus. Postremo, quia hoc negotium orationis, etiam si nostram quoque cooperationem exigat, maiori tamen ex parte pendet a Deo, et est donum Dei. Quare ad hoc potius se anima disponere debet per humilitatem et puritatem, quam confidere in sua praeparatione et industria.
paras.en: Finally, among the things the instructor must attend to is this also: that the exercitant not injure his head by straining too hard in prayer. The danger of this is great — both in time of desolation, when the soul tends to strive harder, as against the current of a river, and in time of consolation, when it gives itself wholly to the favouring winds. It is not enough, therefore, to counsel moderation: for since those making the Exercises are for the most part raw and new to meditation, they cannot well know what will harm them. One must ask what manner they keep in raising the mind to God and in holding it in God, and particularly in the composition of place. And if it appears that they are doing themselves violence, they must be taught the way and manner of thinking gently upon divine things: first, because otherwise it cannot be sustained, and the meditation is hindered; then, because solid fruit consists in the knowledge of those truths and the movement of the will which proceed from inward light — not in this violent straining, nor in those forced tears which Cassian rightly derides; and lastly, because this business of prayer, even though it demands our cooperation too, depends for the greater part on God, and is God's gift. Toward it, therefore, the soul ought rather to dispose itself by humility and purity than trust in its own preparation and industry.
paras.note: The 1919 edition prints 'compositione loci' — the 'composition of place' of the Exercises.

paras.rub: De quibus in universum monendus Instructor
paras.la: Reliqua, quae in universum monendus esset instructor, fere continentur in libro Exercitiorum: partim in meditationibus ipsis, partim in annotationibus, partim etiam in regulis illis discernendi spiritus, quae sunt valde utiles, et quasi lucem praeferunt in omni hoc itinere spirituali, tum prima hebdomada, tum omnibus sequentibus. Et ideo iterum repetendum quod supra attigimus: debere hunc librum admodum familiarem esse instructori, eiusque memoriam renovandam eo tempore quo exercitia traduntur, quia quoties eum leget, toties novum lumen et intelligentiam hauriet.
paras.en: The rest of what the instructor should be advised of in general is mostly contained in the book of the Exercises: partly in the meditations themselves, partly in the Annotations, and partly in those Rules for the Discernment of Spirits, which are most useful and carry a light, as it were, before the whole of this spiritual journey — in the First Week and in all that follow. Hence what we touched on above must be repeated: this book ought to be thoroughly familiar to the instructor, and his memory of it renewed at the very time he is giving the Exercises; for as often as he reads it, so often will he draw from it new light and understanding.

paras.rub: Quando mutare liceat ordinem ac methodum
paras.la: In quo etiam admonendus est: etiamsi ex una parte omnem eius ordinem ac methodum et particularia documenta exacte servare debeat — et quo exactius servabit, eo magis concurret Dominus — tamen ex altera parte multa permitti eius prudentiae, pro varietate vel personarum quae faciunt exercitia, vel spirituum quibus agitantur: ut vel ista exercitia moderari, vel etiam aliqua alia praesenti eorum necessitati opportuna praescribere possit, ut aperte dicitur Annotatione 17 et 18 ex primis, et alibi.
