Since, therefore, the life of Christ is most perfect, and the very idea of virtue and holiness, it follows that the nearer our life comes to it by imitation, the more perfect it too becomes — indeed, the nearer it comes to its own last end, and therefore the happier it is as well.

paras.la: Propter hanc causam haec secunda hebdomada respondet viae illuminativae: quia Christus est sol iustitiae, qui illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum, et ad hoc venit, ut illuminaret sedentes in tenebris et umbra mortis. Et quoniam peccata et pravae affectiones obtenebrant animam, eamque impediunt et retrahunt a Christi imitatione, ideo haec prius eradicanda ex corde erant primis illis exercitiis et meditationibus.
paras.en: For this reason this Second Week corresponds to the illuminative way: for Christ is the sun of justice, who enlightens every man coming into this world, and for this he came — to give light to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. And since sins and depraved affections darken the soul and hinder and hold it back from the imitation of Christ, these had first to be rooted out of the heart by those first exercises and meditations.

paras.rub: Quaenam dispositio in facientibus haec exercitia requirebatur a S. P. N.
paras.la: Dispositio quam P. N. Ignatius requirebat in iis qui facturi essent exercitia huius hebdomadae, est ut ostendant fervorem ac desiderium progrediendi ulterius ad deliberandum de statu vitae. Quare qui hoc nollet, vel tepide vellet, etiam si cuperet progredi in meditationibus, melius esset eum differre ad unum aut alterum mensem. Hoc enim negotium eiusmodi est, ut nisi cum fervore spiritus suscipiatur, non possit habere bonum successum: requirit enim magnum et fortem et constantem animum, qui ex augmento devotionis proveniat.
paras.en: The disposition which Our Father Ignatius required in those who were to make the exercises of this Week is that they show fervour and a desire to go further, to deliberate about their state of life. Hence, if someone were unwilling, or only lukewarmly willing — even though he desired to go on with the meditations — it would be better to put him off for a month or two. For this business is of such a kind that unless it is undertaken with fervour of spirit it cannot have a good outcome: it requires a great, strong and constant soul, arising from an increase of devotion.

paras.rub: Quando quis non est admodum capax
paras.la: Verum est quod, si quis esset a quo nihil magnum sperari posset, quia non esset admodum capax, vel impeditus esset statu matrimonii, posset pro eius captu aliquid addi de sequentibus hebdomadis, ut dirigatur in statu in quo est ad bene vivendum in eo.
paras.en: It is true that if there were someone from whom nothing great could be hoped, because he was not very capable, or was bound by the state of matrimony, something from the following Weeks could be added according to his capacity, so that he may be directed, in the state in which he is, to living well in it.

paras.la: Ceteros autem melius est relinquere cum fame, ut sciant adhuc sibi restare aliquid quod faciant. Contingit enim saepe ut hac dilatione experientia ipsa apertius eis detegat suas necessitates et infirmitates; quod facit ut deinde ardentiores et magis dispositi redeant.
paras.en: The others, however, it is better to leave with an appetite, that they may know there still remains something for them to do. For it often happens that by this delay experience itself uncovers to them more plainly their needs and weaknesses; and this makes them return afterwards more ardent and better disposed.

kapitel.label: Cap. XIX
kapitel.la_titel: De primis quatuor exercitiis secundae hebdomadae
kapitel.en_titel: On the first four exercises of the Second Week

paras.rub: Primum exercitium secundae hebdomadae quid sit
paras.la: Primum exercitium in hac secunda hebdomada est de Regno Christi, quod tamen non computatur inter meditationes, quia prima est de Incarnatione Domini. Est igitur quasi fundamentum quoddam aut prooemium totius huius tractatus, et summa ac compendium vitae et operum Christi Domini in eo negotio quod ei commiserat Pater; de quo Esaias: Opus illius coram eo (Is. 62, 11); et ipse Dominus: Opus quod dedisti mihi ut facerem (Ioan. 17, 4). Et statim addit quidnam id esset: Clarificavi te super terram, manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus (Ioan. 17, 4. 6). Vocat autem omnes homines in societatem tanti et tam gloriosi operis, unumquemque iuxta suum gradum. Ex quo iam incipit apparere diversitas graduum in imitatione Christi.
paras.en: The first exercise in this Second Week is on the Kingdom of Christ; yet it is not counted among the meditations, since the first of these is on the Incarnation of the Lord. It is, then, a kind of foundation or preface to this whole treatise, and a summary and compendium of the life and works of Christ the Lord in that business which the Father had entrusted to him — of which Isaiah says: His work is before him (Is 62:11); and the Lord himself: The work which you gave me to do (John 17:4). And he adds at once what that was: I have glorified you upon earth; I have manifested your name to men (John 17:4, 6). Now he calls all men into the fellowship of so great and so glorious a work, each according to his degree. And from this there already begins to appear the diversity of degrees in the imitation of Christ.

paras.la: Dispositio autem quae requiritur in anima eius qui facit exercitia haec est: ut, quantum est ex sua parte, tendat in id quod perfectius est, si Dominus dederit gratiam et vires. Unde aperte colligitur ex hoc iam loco animam incipere praeparari et disponi ad electionem status, quae postea suo loco expressius proponetur. Sic enim mirabili quodam artificio Spiritus Sancti hic anima excitatur ad perfectionem, ut deinde hanc eandem perfectionem eliciat et indaget in omnibus sequentibus meditationibus, Incarnationis, Nativitatis et aliarum; et ita perfectionis semina, quae hic sparguntur, per illas deinde meditationes latenter crescant et promoveantur, donec in tempore electionis suum fructum ferant. Atque hoc bene notandum est instructori pro sua directione: non quod de hoc monere debeat exercitantem, sed potius sinat res ipsas per se in eius anima operari vimque suam exercere.
paras.en: The disposition required in the soul of the one making the Exercises is this: that, so far as lies in him, he tend toward what is more perfect, if the Lord shall give grace and strength. From this it is plainly gathered that already at this point the soul begins to be prepared and disposed for the election of a state of life, which later, in its own place, will be proposed more expressly. For thus, by a wonderful artifice of the Holy Spirit, the soul is here stirred toward perfection, so that it may afterwards draw out and search for this same perfection in all the following meditations — the Incarnation, the Nativity, and the others; and so the seeds of perfection sown here grow secretly through those meditations and are advanced, until at the time of the election they bear their fruit. And this the instructor should note well for his own direction: not that he should tell the exercitant about it, but rather let the things themselves work in his soul by themselves and exert their own power.

paras.la: Neque hoc tamen impedit quin haec meditatio, sicut etiam quae deinde sequetur de duobus vexillis, tradi possit etiam iis qui non sunt facturi electionem, quoniam etiam hi ea iuvari possunt: siquidem in genere tantum agunt de iis quae ad maiorem Dei gloriam ab unoquoque fieri possunt in Dei obsequio, pro cuiusque capacitate.
paras.en: Nor does this prevent this meditation — like that which follows later, on the Two Standards — from being given also to those who are not going to make an election, since these too can be helped by it: for both treat only in general of the things that can be done by each one, for the greater glory of God, in God's service, according to each one's capacity.

paras.rub: Quare in secunda hebdomada addatur unum praeludium
paras.la: In hac secunda hebdomada notandum est addi hic unum praeludium. Nam cum in prima hebdomada primum praeludium sit constitutio loci, hic ante constitutionem loci ponitur quaedam repraesentatio historiae seu mysterii quod meditandum occurrit. Hoc autem non ita intelligendum est, ut tunc immorari debeamus in meditando illo mysterio — sic enim nihil differret praeludium a meditatione — sed ita est accipiendum: ut in primo illo praeludio proponatur historia generatim et quasi tota in communi, ut sciatur materia de qua tunc cogitandum est, et anima incipiat in ea actuari et ad eam elevari; deinde vero in ipsa meditatione incipiat in singulis eius partibus immorari, easque ponderare et penetrare. Ut cum quis coniicit oculos in tabulam aliquam pictam, in qua sit varietas rerum pictarum: prius unico intuitu omnia confuse cernit, et scit quid in ea tabula contineatur; postea vero figit oculos in singulis particularibus rebus quae ibi pictae sunt, easque sigillatim melius et accuratius perpendit.
paras.en: In this Second Week it should be noted that one prelude is here added. For whereas in the First Week the first prelude is the composition of place, here before the composition of place there is set a certain representation of the history, or mystery, that comes up for meditation. This is not to be understood as though we ought then to linger in meditating on that mystery — for then the prelude would differ in nothing from the meditation — but is to be taken thus: in that first prelude the history is proposed in general, and as it were whole and in common, so that the matter to be thought upon may be known, and the soul may begin to be engaged in it and raised toward it; then, in the meditation itself, it begins to dwell on its several parts, and to weigh and penetrate them. Just as when someone casts his eyes on a painted panel in which there is a variety of things depicted: at first, with a single glance, he sees everything indistinctly, and knows what the panel contains; but afterwards he fixes his eyes on the particular things painted there, one by one, and considers them singly, better and more exactly.

paras.la: Quod autem attinet ad puncta harum meditationum, sumenda erunt in fine libelli exercitiorum, ubi mysteria vitae Christi ordine posita sunt, distincta fere singula tribus punctis; etsi simplicioribus, qui ea non legerint aut legere non possint in Evangeliis, explicatius tradi oportebit, addita brevi declaratione, ut dicitur secunda annotatione ex viginti. Unde quod in meditatione Incarnationis et Nativitatis etiam dicitur de contemplandis personis et earum verbis et operibus, intelligi debet referendo ad illam quam diximus distributionem quae in fine libri ponitur: nempe cogitando haec in singulis punctis, ut occurrunt ordine suo — non autem quod necessarium sit omnes prius personas totius mysterii, deinde omnia verba eiusdem, ac demum opera separatim meditari; hoc enim, praesertim in quibusdam meditationibus, pareret confusionem.
paras.en: As for the points of these meditations, they are to be taken from the end of the little book of the Exercises, where the mysteries of the life of Christ are set out in order, almost every one divided into three points; though for the simpler sort, who have not read them, or cannot read them, in the Gospels, they will have to be delivered more fully, with a brief explanation added, as is said in the second of the twenty Annotations. Hence what is also said in the meditation on the Incarnation and the Nativity about contemplating the persons and their words and deeds must be understood by reference to that distribution, which we have mentioned, placed at the end of the book: namely, by thinking on these things in the several points as they occur in their order — not that it is necessary to meditate first on all the persons of the whole mystery, then on all its words, and lastly on the deeds separately; for this, especially in certain meditations, would breed confusion.

paras.la: Quare hoc tantum voluit P. Ignatius: regulam dare, in singulis punctis quo meditantis intentio ferri debeat — primum quidem in ipsas personas quae in illo puncto occurrant, tum ad verba, si prius verba, vel ad facta, si prius occurrant facta. Et ita, absoluto uno puncto, transeatur ad aliud, eundem ordinem in eo servando.
paras.en: Father Ignatius, then, intended only this: to give a rule as to where, in each point, the attention of the one meditating should be directed — first indeed to the persons themselves who occur in that point, then to the words, if words come first, or to the deeds, if deeds occur first. And so, one point being finished, let him pass to another, keeping the same order in it.

paras.la: Caeterum, etsi hic tantum mentio fit de his tribus, non tamen prohibetur quin possint etiam addi alia puncta: ut v. g. cogitationes et affectus personarum interiores, tum etiam virtutes, et praeterea modus et finis mysteriorum quae occurrunt, causa item et effectus, tempus et reliquae circunstantiae — ut foecundior sit meditatio, et maior eius fructus.
paras.en: For the rest, although mention is made here only of these three, it is not forbidden that other points also be added: as, for example, the interior thoughts and affections of the persons, then also their virtues, and further the manner and end of the mysteries that occur, likewise their cause and effect, the time, and the remaining circumstances — that the meditation may be more fruitful, and its fruit greater.

kapitel.label: Cap. XX
kapitel.la_titel: De quinto exercitio secundae hebdomadae, quod est applicatio sensuum
kapitel.en_titel: On the fifth exercise of the Second Week, which is the application of the senses

paras.rub: De quinto exercitio, videlicet de applicatione sensuum
paras.la: Exercitium quintum, quod est applicatio sensuum, est facile valde et utile: imaginando nos videre personas, et audire verba aut strepitum si qui fit, vel tangere aut osculari sive loca sive personas — quod tamen fieri debet cum omni reverentia et modestia ac timore. Olfactum P. N. Ignatius refert ad odorandam fragrantiam animae ex donis Dei, et gustum ad gustandum eius dulcedinem; quod utrunque significat praesentiam quandam rei vel personarum quas meditamur, cum gustu et amore earum tenero.
paras.en: The fifth exercise, which is the application of the senses, is very easy and useful: imagining that we see the persons, and hear the words, or any sound there may be, or touch or kiss either the places or the persons — which, however, must be done with all reverence and modesty and fear. The sense of smell Our Father Ignatius refers to smelling the fragrance of the soul that comes from the gifts of God, and taste to tasting its sweetness; both of which signify a certain presence of the thing or persons on whom we meditate, with relish and a tender love of them.

paras.rub: Intelligentia illius notandi, post meditationes de Incarnatione et Nativitate faciendam esse applicationem sensuum
paras.la: Quod autem hic dicitur — facta meditatione Incarnationis et Nativitatis, faciendam deinde separatim hanc applicationem sensuum — intelligendum est idem deinceps fieri debere in reliquis meditationibus vitae Christi. Quod non ita accipiendum est, quasi hanc applicationem debeamus habere seiunctam ab omni materia meditationis, sed ut praecipuus scopus circa mysterii considerationem sit sensuum applicatio.
paras.en: As for what is said here — that after the meditation on the Incarnation and the Nativity this application of the senses is then to be made separately — it is to be understood that the same must be done thereafter in the remaining meditations on the life of Christ. This is not to be taken as though we ought to keep this application detached from all the matter of the meditation, but in the sense that, in considering the mystery, the chief aim should be the application of the senses.

paras.rub: In quo differt applicatio sensuum a meditatione
paras.la: Differt autem applicatio ista sensuum a meditatione, quoniam meditatio est magis intellectualis, et magis versatur in ratiocinatione, et omnino est altior: discurrit enim per causas illorum mysteriorum et effecta, et in eis investigat attributa Dei, ut bonitatem, sapientiam, charitatem et reliqua. At vero applicatio non discurrit, sed tantum inhaeret in illis sensibilibus, ut in aspectu et auditu et reliquis eiusmodi, quibus fruitur et delectatur cum profectu spirituali.
paras.en: This application of the senses differs from meditation in that meditation is more intellectual, is more occupied with reasoning, and is altogether higher: for it runs through the causes and effects of those mysteries, and searches in them the attributes of God — goodness, wisdom, charity and the rest. The application, on the other hand, does not reason, but simply rests in those sensible things — in seeing and hearing and the like — enjoying them and taking delight in them, with spiritual profit.

paras.la: Est autem eius duplex utilitas. Interdum enim, cum anima non potest profundiora speculari, dum in his immoratur, paulatim disponitur et elevatur ad illa altiora. Interdum autem contra: anima iam impinguata et fervens devotione ex cognitione illorum mysteriorum altiorum, descendens deinde ad haec sensibilia, in omnibus invenit pastum et consolationem et fructum, ex abundantia amoris — qui facit ut minima quaeque, ac vel ipsi nutus, magnifiant, et materiam amoris et consolationis praebeant.
paras.en: Its usefulness is twofold. Sometimes, when the soul cannot contemplate deeper things, by dwelling on these it is gradually disposed and raised to those higher matters. But sometimes the reverse: the soul, already enriched and fervent with devotion from the knowledge of those higher mysteries, descending then to these sensible things, finds in everything nourishment, consolation and fruit, out of the abundance of love — which makes even the least things, even mere gestures, grow great, and yield matter for love and consolation.

paras.la: In mysteriis Christi tradendis debet instructor ea desumere ex ipso libro exercitiorum, in fine, ubi, ut dictum est, descripta sunt cum suis punctis. Quare qui magis versati sunt in meditando, iis satis erit dictare vel dare in scriptis puncta ut ibi habentur, admonendo ut semper eandem formam teneant quam prima die. Cum aliis autem minus versatis oportebit ad particularia magis descendere, accommodando praeludia ad materiam, et introducendo eos, ut sciant sibi proponere personas cum suis circumstantiis, tum earum verba et facta, etc.
paras.en: In giving the mysteries of Christ the instructor should take them from the book of the Exercises itself, at the end, where, as has been said, they are set out with their points. For those more practised in meditating it will therefore suffice to dictate the points, or give them in writing, as they stand there, with the reminder always to keep the same form as on the first day. With others, less practised, it will be necessary to descend more to particulars, adapting the preludes to the matter, and leading them in, so that they know how to set before themselves the persons with their circumstances, then their words and deeds, and so forth.

kapitel.label: Cap. XXI
kapitel.la_titel: De meditationum horis, lectione spirituali et eo qui exercetur visitando
kapitel.en_titel: On the hours of the meditations, spiritual reading, and visiting the exercitant

paras.la: Si is qui se exercet fatigatus videatur — immo etiam si non adeo fatigatus sit, tamen ut melius durare possit — expedit ut detur illi aliqua relaxatio in horis meditandi; et tunc omitti poterit meditatio quae fit media nocte, et retineri aliae quatuor horae.
paras.en: If the exercitant seems fatigued — or even if he is not so fatigued, still, that he may hold out the better — it is expedient to grant him some relaxation in the hours of meditation; and then the meditation made at midnight may be omitted, and the other four hours retained.
paras.note: Margin cross-reference: 'Ex notabili unico in die secundo 2. hebdomadae.'

paras.la: Potest etiam in hac hebdomada et sequentibus, post absolutas meditationes, reliquo tempore legi aliquis liber — sed eiusmodi qui pietatem potius nutriat, quam intellectum novitatibus exerceat: ut sunt aliqua ex operibus S. Bernardi, vel Gerson de imitatione Christi, vel Granata. Si vero liber hic contineret aliquem tractatum de Christi mysteriis, non expediret ut ea legerentur de quibus postea faciendae sunt meditationes, sed de quibus iam factae sunt, vel quae eo die sunt faciendae.
paras.en: In this Week and the following ones, after the meditations are finished, some book may also be read in the remaining time — but of the kind that nourishes piety rather than exercises the intellect with novelties: such as some of the works of St. Bernard, or Gerson On the Imitation of Christ, or Granada. But if this book should contain a treatise on the mysteries of Christ, it would not be expedient to read those on which meditations are afterwards to be made, but those on which they have already been made, or are to be made that day.
paras.note: 'Gerson de imitatione Christi' reflects the sixteenth-century attribution of the Imitation of Christ to Jean Gerson (now ascribed to Thomas à Kempis); 'Granata' is Luis de Granada.

paras.la: Quod attinet ad visitandum eum qui exercetur: semel saltem esset visitandus in die, excepto tempore electionis, quo tempore solent incidere frequentiores desolationes et perplexitates, quae crebriorem visitationem requirunt.
paras.en: As to visiting the one making the Exercises: he should be visited at least once a day, except during the time of the election, when more frequent desolations and perplexities are wont to occur, which require more frequent visiting.

kapitel.label: Cap. XXII
kapitel.la_titel: De electione, quanti momenti sit, et quis ordo in hac materia servandus
kapitel.en_titel: On the election: of what moment it is, and what order is to be kept in this matter

paras.la: In omnibus exercitiis nullus est difficilior locus, aut qui maiorem dexteritatem et discretionem spiritualem requirat, quam electionis: quoniam hoc tempus expositum est diversis motibus animi, et saepe etiam erroribus, cum homo non solum a malo vincatur, sed plerunque etiam boni et recti imagine fallatur.
paras.en: In all the Exercises there is no more difficult place, nor one that requires greater skill and spiritual discretion, than that of the election: for this time is exposed to diverse movements of the soul, and often also to errors, since a man is not only overcome by evil, but very often deceived by the appearance of what is good and right.

paras.la: In hac ergo materia illud ante omnia intelligendum videtur, et ante oculos tenendum: quanti referat eligere statum vitae. Nam si homo, ut rationalis, debet omnibus suis actionibus ponere finem congruentem rationi, Christianus autem debet omnia opera sua dirigere ad finem supernaturalem: si haec ergo in singulis actibus fieri debent, quanto magis in capiendo statu, ex quo scilicet consequuntur fere omnia opera vitae nostrae — ita ut, si finis ipsius status sit vitiosus, ea etiam quae ad finem consequuntur oporteat esse vitiosa.
paras.en: In this matter, then, this above all must be understood and kept before the eyes: how much it matters to choose a state of life. For if man, as a rational being, must set for all his actions an end agreeable to reason, and the Christian must direct all his works to a supernatural end — if this must be done in each single act, how much more in taking up a state, from which follow nearly all the works of our life; so that, if the end of the state itself is vicious, the things that follow toward that end must be vicious too.

paras.la: Deinde, ut in corpore animantis plura sunt membra, neque omnia membra sunt oculus, aut omnia pedes, ut ait S. Paulus (1 Cor. 12), ita in hoc corpore Ecclesiae oportet esse varios gradus et status. Huius autem divisionis et partitionis auctor est Spiritus Sanctus, ad quem pertinet singulis suum locum tribuere. Unde Apostolus eodem loco: Divisiones gratiarum sunt, idem autem Spiritus; et divisiones ministeriorum sunt, idem autem Dominus; et divisiones operationum, idem vero Deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus (1 Cor. 12, 4-6). Ex quo constat: ut famuli a suo Domino suo quisque operi ac muneri destinantur, sic homines a Deo; ac proinde non debere hominem impedire in seipso id quod Deus in eo et de eo agere vult, sed oportere ut ei fideliter serviat in quacunque re eius maiestas voluerit.
paras.en: Further, as in the body of a living creature there are many members, and not all the members are an eye, nor all feet, as St. Paul says (1 Cor 12), so in this body of the Church there must be various degrees and states. And the author of this division and apportionment is the Holy Spirit, to whom it belongs to assign to each his place. Hence the Apostle in the same place: There are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit; and diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and diversities of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all (1 Cor 12:4-6). From this it is clear that, as servants are appointed by their master each to his own work and office, so are men by God; and consequently a man ought not to hinder in himself what God wills to do in him and with him, but should serve him faithfully in whatever thing his Majesty shall will.

paras.la: Accedit etiam propria utilitas, eaque magna, quoniam pertinet ad salutem aeternam. Nam etsi Deus nemini negat auxilium necessarium ad salutem, tamen non est dubium quin iis multo abundantius gratiam suam et lumen atque opem communicet, qui non se in aliquem vitae statum ex libito suo intruserunt, sed eum elegerunt quem, praemissa diligenti consideratione, putarunt esse iuxta divinum beneplacitum.
paras.en: There is besides one's own advantage, and that a great one, since it concerns eternal salvation. For although God denies no one the help necessary for salvation, there is no doubt that he communicates his grace and light and aid much more abundantly to those who have not thrust themselves into some state of life at their own pleasure, but have chosen the one which, after diligent consideration, they judged to be according to the divine good pleasure.

paras.rub: Dei, non autem nostra, sequenda voluntas
paras.la: Denique, si nos in tanta re nostro iudicio ac placito gubernare velimus, facile in maximos et maxime perniciosos errores incidemus; si vero Dei voluntatem executi fuerimus, ille, ut Pater et Creator noster, nihil de nobis statuet quod nobis utile et salutare non sit — immo vero etiam aptum et accommodatum nobis, quoniam ipse noscit figmentum nostrum.
paras.en: Finally, if in so great a matter we choose to govern ourselves by our own judgment and pleasure, we shall easily fall into the greatest and most pernicious errors; but if we carry out the will of God, he, as our Father and Creator, will determine nothing concerning us that is not useful and salutary for us — nay, even fitted and suited to us, for he himself knows the clay of which we are made.

paras.la: Haec igitur et alia in hanc sententiam non solum instructori utilia erunt, ut in hoc negotio magnum studium adhibeat, sed multo magis ei qui facit exercitia, ut videat quo animo aggredi debeat rem adeo necessariam.
paras.en: These things, then, and others to the same purpose, will be useful not only to the instructor, that he may apply great care in this business, but much more to the one making the Exercises, that he may see with what spirit he ought to approach so necessary a matter.

paras.la: Igitur, ut in hoc tractando aliquis ordo servetur: primo dicemus quales esse debeant qui ad electionem admittuntur; secundo, quales ii qui eos dirigunt; tertio, quae sint res de quibus est electio; quarto, quae in ea regulae servandae; quinto, quis sit ordo et praxis electionis faciendae.
paras.en: So then, that some order may be kept in treating this: first we shall say what sort of persons those should be who are admitted to the election; second, what sort those who direct them; third, what the things are about which the election is made; fourth, what rules are to be observed in it; fifth, what is the order and practice of making the election.

kapitel.label: Cap. XXIII
kapitel.la_titel: Quales esse debeant qui ad electionem admittantur
kapitel.en_titel: What sort of persons should be admitted to the election

paras.la: Circa primum, apertum est non omnes esse admittendos ad electionem status. Qui enim iam tenent statum determinatum, ut coniugati aut religiosi, non debent de hoc agere, sed tantum iuvari debent, ut in suo quisque statu ad perfectionem tendat, pro mensura gratiae quam ei Dominus Deus concedat. Qui autem adhuc statum non habent, non tamen omnibus indifferenter dari debet electio, ut habetur in septima parte Constitutionum, cap. 4, lit. F, ubi dicitur quod non nisi paucis, iisque huiusmodi, ut ex eorum profectu non vulgaris ad Dei gloriam fructus speretur. Igitur qui vel incapaces essent huius perfectionis — cuiusmodi sunt leves natura et inconstantes, quos in primis explorare oportebit nec ullo modo admittere ad electionem — aut quos constet habere passiones quasdam indomitas, aut malos habitus qui videantur incorrigibiles, non essent admittendi, nisi tam certa signa essent peculiaris cuiusdam gratiae, ut haec omnia suppleret.
paras.en: As to the first point, it is plain that not all are to be admitted to the election of a state. Those who already hold a fixed state, such as the married or religious, should not treat of this, but should only be helped so that each, in his own state, may tend toward perfection according to the measure of grace which the Lord God grants him. As for those who do not yet have a state, the election should nevertheless not be given to all indiscriminately, as is laid down in the Seventh Part of the Constitutions, chapter 4, letter F, where it is said that it should be given only to a few, and to such that from their progress no ordinary fruit for the glory of God may be hoped. Therefore those who would be incapable of this perfection — such as the naturally light-minded and inconstant, whom above all one must test, and by no means admit to the election — or those known to have certain untamed passions, or bad habits that appear incorrigible, should not be admitted, unless there were such sure signs of some special grace as would make up for all this.

paras.la: Secundo, praeter naturam et mores aptos, requiritur etiam ut ille cui datur electio eam ipse desideret et petat. Et hoc omnino necessarium est, et nullo modo alioquin dari debet, multo autem minus ingeri et obtrudi non cupienti. Nam, praeterquam quod qui sic affectus est omnia quae ei dicentur cum suspicione accipiet, et ideo iis iuvari non poterit, est etiam ea causa: quod in electione facienda multae et magnae incidunt difficultates, etiam cum voluntas bona et fervens est; quare multo erunt maiores cum voluntas languet, et ideo nunquam eas superare poterit.
paras.en: Second, besides an apt nature and character, it is also required that the one to whom the election is given should himself desire and ask for it. This is altogether necessary; otherwise it should in no way be given — much less thrust and forced upon one who does not want it. For besides the fact that a person so disposed will receive everything said to him with suspicion, and so cannot be helped by it, there is also this reason: in making the election many great difficulties arise even when the will is good and fervent; they will be far greater when the will languishes, and then he will never be able to overcome them.

paras.rub: Electurus sit ab omni affectu liber
paras.la: Tertio, valde expedit ut qui ingreditur electionem studeat esse liber ab omni affectu inordinato, et plane ad omnia indifferens, ad hoc vero unum inclinatus: ut sanctum Dei beneplacitum sequatur, quodcunque illud esse cognoverit. Quare si cerneretur eum nimis propendere ad divitias, minus autem ad paupertatem, non esset bene dispositus, nec sperandus esset bonus exitus in electione. Ille enim affectus, aversus a via perfectiori et ad imperfectiorem conversus, intellectum traheret ad excogitandas rationes tali affectui consentaneas; ac cum, ut dici solet, quicquid recipitur, recipiatur ad modum recipientis, facile fieret ut existimaret illam esse Dei voluntatem quae est ipsius voluntas. Oportet igitur ut perveniat ad tertium gradum humilitatis, qui ponitur in libro exercitiorum, aut saltem ad secundum; cui comparando serviunt meditationes de vexillis et de tribus classibus et aliae, de quibus infra dicetur. Et ideo esset in iis meditationibus diutius retinendus, ut paulatim disponatur ad hoc aequilibrium animi — partim conando propria diligentia, partim id a Deo petendo ferventibus orationibus. Quod si ad hanc resignationem et indifferentiam non pervenerit, tota tractatio de modo eligendi relinquenda est; et tunc, si ita expedire videbitur, procedendum in reliquis exercitiis faciendis, ut, si fieri potest, per ea ad maiorem maturitatem perducatur, vel post breve tempus finis eis imponendus.
paras.en: Third, it is highly expedient that whoever enters upon the election strive to be free from every inordinate affection, and entirely indifferent to all things, inclined to this one thing alone: to follow God's holy good pleasure, whatever he shall know it to be. Hence if it were seen that he leaned too much toward riches and less toward poverty, he would not be well disposed, nor could a good outcome of the election be hoped for. For that affection, turned away from the more perfect way and toward the less perfect, would drag the understanding into devising reasons agreeable to such an affection; and since, as the saying goes, whatever is received is received after the manner of the receiver, it would easily come about that he judged that to be God's will which is his own will. He must therefore arrive at the third degree of humility set down in the book of the Exercises, or at least at the second; and to acquiring this serve the meditations on the Standards and on the Three Classes, and others of which we shall speak below. He should therefore be kept longer in those meditations, that he may gradually be disposed toward this equilibrium of soul — partly by striving with his own diligence, partly by asking it of God in fervent prayers. But if he does not arrive at this resignation and indifference, the whole treatment of the manner of electing is to be laid aside; and then, if it seems expedient, one should proceed with the remaining exercises, so that, if possible, he may be brought by them to greater maturity — or after a short time an end should be put to them.

paras.la: Quarto, omnium optima est illa dispositio: ut non modo non magis propendeat ad terrena retinenda, sed, quoad fieri potest, voluntatem suam semper inflectere conetur ad id quod perfectius est. Nam licet re ipsa non id electurus sit, quia fortasse Deus non eum vocet ad talem statum, tamen nihil ei nocebit, immo plurimum proderit tale desiderium; ac proinde in his exercitiis semper proponitur via perfectior, tamquam magis optanda et a Deo petenda. In quo valde notanda est sententia quaedam P. N. Ignatii, quae inventa est in quodam eius scripto, ubi ita ait: debere instructorem ita disponere eum qui est in exercitiis, ut omnino resignatus sit, tam ad consilia sequenda quam ad praecepta, immo vero, quantum in ipso est, magis inclinatus sit ad consilia, si id maius Dei obsequium fuerit. Et addit: maiora utique signa requiri ad statuendum quod ea sit Dei voluntas, ut quis in eo statu maneat in quo satis sit servare praecepta, quam ut viam consiliorum ingrediatur — quia Dominus tam aperte ad consilia exhortatus est, at vero in illo statu magna ostendit esse pericula.
paras.en: Fourth, the best disposition of all is this: not only that he not lean more toward keeping earthly things, but that, as far as may be, he strive always to bend his will toward what is more perfect. For though in fact he may not choose it — since perhaps God does not call him to such a state — such a desire will do him no harm, indeed it will profit him greatly; and hence in these Exercises the more perfect way is always set forth as the more to be desired and to be asked of God. Here a saying of Our Father Ignatius is much to be noted, found in a certain writing of his, where he says: the instructor ought so to dispose the one who is in the Exercises that he be wholly resigned, as ready to follow the counsels as the precepts — nay, so far as in him lies, more inclined to the counsels, if that should be the greater service of God. And he adds: greater signs indeed are required to conclude that it is God's will that someone remain in that state in which it is enough to keep the precepts, than that he enter the way of the counsels — because the Lord exhorted so plainly to the counsels, whereas in that other state he showed there are great dangers.

paras.la: Ultima est ea dispositio quam idem P. Ignatius eodem loco praecipit: nempe ut qui facit electionem colligat se totum intra se, et toto tempore quo durat haec deliberatio claudat sensus, claudat animum omnibus aliis rebus, nihilque velit videre aut audire quod non de sursum sit. Quibus verbis duo indicantur. Primum, ut anima non sinat se distrahi ad alias cogitationes, sed hoc unum agat et huic uni intenta sit, ceteris omnibus negociis a se reiectis. Alterum est, ut in hac deliberatione non admittat rationes quae non sint e caelo — id est nullas admittat quae sapiant carnem et sanguinem, aut aliquid humanum ac terrenum — quia omnia manare debent ex uno illo principio, quod est desiderium gloriae Dei et exequendi eius voluntatem. Hic enim est verus ille sumptus ad aedificandam turrim, de qua est in Evangelio (Luc. 14); et hoc magnam animae fiduciam affert, quod Deus non sinet eam decipi: quia, cum eum in toto corde et in veritate quaerat, nunquam se Deus ab ea avertet — cuius scilicet tanta est bonitas et amor in suam creaturam, ut etiam occurrat saepe non quaerentibus. Quod licet ita sit, et ea sit perfecta electio ad quam solius Dei amor impellit, tamen si praecipuus quidem esset amor Dei, sed praeter illum aliquid etiam accederet quod eodem inclinaret — modo non repugnans Dei legi ac voluntati, et ex sua natura bonum, utputa consolatio propria et quies spiritualis, ratio valetudinis, aut aliquid eiusmodi — non propterea improbanda esset electio. Haec tamen oporteret semper minus esse praecipua, et minus praecipue movere, et haec ipsa ad Dei amorem referri.
paras.en: The last disposition is the one which the same Father Ignatius prescribes in the same place: namely, that he who makes the election gather himself wholly within himself, and for the whole time this deliberation lasts close his senses, close his mind to all other things, and wish to see or hear nothing that is not from above. By these words two things are indicated. First, that the soul not allow itself to be drawn off to other thoughts, but do this one thing and be intent on this one thing, all other business cast aside. The second is that in this deliberation it admit no reasons that are not from heaven — that is, admit none that savour of flesh and blood, or of anything human and earthly — because everything must flow from that one principle which is the desire of God's glory and of carrying out his will. For this is that true cost of building the tower of which the Gospel speaks (Luke 14); and it brings the soul great confidence that God will not allow it to be deceived: for since it seeks him with its whole heart and in truth, God will never turn away from it — he whose goodness and love toward his creature are so great that he often comes even to meet those who do not seek him. And though this is so, and that is the perfect election to which the love of God alone impels, yet if the love of God were indeed the chief motive, but besides it something else were added inclining the same way — provided it is not contrary to God's law and will, and is good in its own nature, such as one's own consolation and spiritual rest, considerations of health, or something of that kind — the election would not on that account be condemned. These, however, must always be less principal, move less principally, and themselves be referred to the love of God.
paras.note: Margin: 'Annot. 16 ex 20.'

kapitel.label: Cap. XXIV
kapitel.la_titel: Qualis esse debeat qui dirigit electionem
kapitel.en_titel: What sort of person he should be who directs the election

paras.la: Circa secundum: officium eius qui tradit exercitia, in hoc particulari negocio, est cooperari motioni divinae, eamque non praeire sed sequi, et ad hoc disponere animam eius qui facit exercitia, removendo impedimenta — nempe errores, dolos, affectiones atque inclinationes inordinatas. Non debet eum movere vel ad unam vel ad aliam partem, ut dicitur in 15. annotatione ex prioribus. Etsi enim ex natura sua licitum est, ac meritorium etiam, hortari ad perfectiora, tamen, ut eiusmodi deliberationes solidius fiant, et sine ulla humana persuasione, multo melius est permittere ut solus Deus cum sua creatura tractet, nec aliquis tertius intercedat; et hoc maxime in exercitiis, ubi se anima ad hoc ipsum disponit. Ratio huius est, quia electio tantae rei, ut est status vitae, non debet niti persuasione aut inductione humana, sed sola Dei voluntate; alioqui metuendum esset illud quod Dominus dixit: Omnis plantatio quam non plantavit Pater meus caelestis eradicabitur (Matth. 15, 13). Et cum in eiusmodi via, per se ardua et deinde daemonum invidiae exposita, sine dubio secuturae sint multae tentationes ac difficultates, non potest ullum auxilium ac sublevatio expectari ab homine qui nos induxit, nisi levemus oculos nostros in caelum, et dicere possimus: Dominus solus dux meus fuit. Quoniam, iuxta Apostolum, sperandum est eum qui dedit velle daturum etiam perficere, et confirmaturum usque in finem (Philip. 2, 13).
paras.en: As to the second point: the office of the one who gives the Exercises, in this particular business, is to cooperate with the divine motion — not to go before it but to follow it — and to dispose for it the soul of the one making the Exercises by removing hindrances: namely errors, deceits, inordinate affections and inclinations. He must not move him to one side or the other, as is said in the fifteenth of the introductory Annotations. For although of its own nature it is lawful, and even meritorious, to exhort to the more perfect, nevertheless, so that such deliberations may be made more solidly, and without any human persuasion, it is far better to allow God alone to deal with his creature, and no third party to come between — and this above all in the Exercises, where the soul is disposing itself for this very thing. The reason for this is that the election of so great a matter as a state of life must rest not on human persuasion or inducement, but on the will of God alone; otherwise one would have to fear the word of the Lord: Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Mt 15:13). And since on such a way — arduous in itself, and moreover exposed to the envy of the demons — many temptations and difficulties will doubtless follow, no help or relief can be expected from the man who led us in, unless we lift up our eyes to heaven and can say: The Lord alone was my guide. For, according to the Apostle, it is to be hoped that he who gave the willing will also give the accomplishing, and will strengthen us to the end (Phil 2:13).

paras.la: Ex quo colligitur eum qui dirigit in hac electione debere ipsum quoque suo modo indifferentem esse, ut fideliter peragat opus quod ei commissum et creditum est, idque tantum respiciat et cupiat, ut Dei voluntas et beneplacitum compleatur, nihil apponens de suo spiritu proprio: hoc enim est immittere falcem in messem Dei. Et praeterea posset aliquando praebere materiam tentationum exercitanti, quia maneret semper aperta daemoni haec porta: suggerendi quod hominis instinctu ad religionem inductus esset. Persuadeat autem sibi illud tutum fore, ac sine periculo, quod indagaverit iuxta regulas sanae electionis. Tantum diligens sit in sublevando ac dirigendo quem Dominus eius curae ac fidei commisit.
paras.en: From this it is gathered that he who directs in this election must himself also be, in his own way, indifferent, so that he may faithfully carry through the work committed and entrusted to him, and look to and desire this alone: that God's will and good pleasure be fulfilled, adding nothing of his own spirit — for that is to put one's sickle into God's harvest. Moreover, he might at times furnish matter for temptations to the exercitant, since this door would always remain open to the demon: to suggest that he was led into religion by a man's prompting. But let him be assured that what has been searched out according to the rules of a sound election will be safe and without danger. Let him only be diligent in supporting and directing the one whom the Lord has committed to his care and trust.
paras.note: Margin: 'Annot. 15 ex 20.'

paras.la: Vigilet in detegendis fraudibus et paralogismis daemonis: quoniam ex falsis principiis, qualia ille suggeret, sequetur non nisi falsa conclusio.
paras.en: Let him be watchful in uncovering the frauds and false reasonings of the demon: for from false principles, such as he will suggest, nothing but a false conclusion will follow.

paras.la: Animadvertat etiam contingere saepe ut quis ingrediatur in electionem cum optima dispositione, et tamen in ipso articulo eligendi insurgat in ipso aliquis sinister affectus, qui omnia perturbet et suffocet bonum semen; et ideo cautus sit et industrius, ad haec omnia tum providenda tum praecavenda.
paras.en: Let him observe, too, that it often happens that someone enters upon the election with the best disposition, and yet at the very moment of choosing some sinister affection rises up in him, which throws everything into disorder and chokes the good seed; and therefore let him be cautious and industrious both to foresee and to forestall all these things.

kapitel.label: Cap. XXV
kapitel.la_titel: Quae sint res de quibus est electio
kapitel.en_titel: What the things are about which the election is made

paras.la: Circa tertium, illud certum est: rem omnem quae sub electionem cadat oportere esse bonam, sive sit negocium aliquod particulare, sive status totius vitae.
paras.en: As to the third point, this is certain: everything that falls under the election must be good, whether it be some particular affair or the state of one's whole life.
paras.note: Margin: 'Ex introductione ad eligendarum rerum notitiam.'

paras.la: Electio autem status versatur circa duo: sitne manendum in praeceptis, an progrediendum ad consilia.
paras.en: The election of a state turns on two things: whether one should remain with the precepts, or go on to the counsels.

paras.la: Si consilia sequenda: num in religione, an extra eam. Quanquam enim vix iam extra religionem servari possunt, tamen potest esse talis natura, ut non sit valde idonea ad communitatem vitae et obedientiam, et tamen possit servare paupertatem et castitatem.
paras.en: If the counsels are to be followed: whether in religion, or outside it. For although they can now scarcely be kept outside religion, still there may be such a temperament as is not very suited to common life and obedience, and yet can keep poverty and chastity.

paras.rub: Si in religionem ingrediendum, quaenam eligenda
paras.la: Tertio, si in religione, restat etiam in particulari quis ordo eligendus: quia alios vocat Dominus ad maiorem solitudinem, alios ad iuvandos proximos, et ipsa naturalis complexio vel corporis vel etiam animae alia alii instituto aptior est.
paras.en: Third, if in religion, there still remains the particular choice of which order: for the Lord calls some to greater solitude, others to the helping of their neighbours; and one's very natural constitution, of body or even of soul, is better suited to one institute than to another.

paras.la: Quarto, electa peculiari religione, deliberatur etiam de tempore et de modo id exequendi.
paras.en: Fourth, when a particular religious order has been chosen, deliberation is also made about the time and the manner of carrying it out.

paras.la: In eligenda hac autem vel illa religione cavendum est primo, ne eligatur aliqua iam corrupta, vel in qua non vigeat observantia. Secundo, inter illas ipsas in quibus viget observantia, praeferenda est ea cuius institutum sit perfectius; in quo diiudicando est optima doctrina sancti Thomae, 2. 2, quaest. 188, art. 6. Et habenda est maxime ratio personae: non solum iuxta vires et propensionem, sed etiam iuxta dotes et talenta quae habet, propter maius Dei obsequium.
paras.en: In choosing this or that religious order, care must be taken first that none be chosen which is already corrupted, or in which observance is not in vigour. Second, among those in which observance flourishes, that one is to be preferred whose institute is the more perfect; and for judging this the teaching of St. Thomas is excellent, 2a 2ae, q. 188, art. 6. And the greatest account must be taken of the person: not only of his strength and inclination, but also of the gifts and talents he has, for the greater service of God.

paras.la: In tempore autem exequendi divinam vocationem est interdum peculiaris difficultas: quoniam in his quae repugnant sensui solet humana infirmitas procrastinare quantum potest, et causas morarum innectere, seque ipsam decipere, quaerendo rationes differendi. Quare optimum est hanc ipsam difficultatem profligare in exercitiis, et cogitare quod ait sanctus Ambrosius: Nescit tarda molimina Spiritus Sancti gratia. Imitanda est etiam promptitudo Apostolorum, relictis statim retibus et patre; valetque illa ratio: Si aliquando, cur non modo? et si non modo, fortasse nunquam. Nunc enim recens est Dei motio et eius auxilium; postea vero facile fieri potest — et fit quotidie — ut refrigescat hic spiritus, et sic multo difficilius erit resistere pugnae carnis et diaboli. Et haec de electione consiliorum.
paras.en: In the timing of carrying out the divine vocation there is sometimes a peculiar difficulty: for in things repugnant to sense, human weakness is wont to procrastinate as long as it can, to weave excuses for delay, and to deceive itself by seeking reasons for putting off. It is therefore best to defeat this very difficulty within the Exercises, and to reflect on the saying of St. Ambrose: The grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow undertakings. The promptness of the Apostles is also to be imitated, who at once left their nets and their father; and that argument holds: If at some time, why not now? and if not now, perhaps never. For now the motion of God and his help are fresh; afterwards it may easily happen — and happens daily — that this spirit grows cold, and then it will be much harder to withstand the assault of the flesh and the devil. So much for the election of the counsels.

paras.rub: Quid, si quis eligat servare praecepta
paras.la: Si quis vero eligat servare praecepta, restat adhuc consultandum in quo statu, aut in qua ratione vivendi, ea servet: quae singula discutienda sunt, ut eo melius et cum maiori luce vita instituatur.
paras.en: But if someone chooses to keep the precepts, it still remains to consider in what state, or in what manner of living, he is to keep them; and each of these points must be examined, so that his life may be ordered the better and with greater light.

paras.rub: In aliis particularibus utendum iisdem regulis
paras.la: Denique in aliis particularibus negociis — ut in suscipienda aliqua re vel non suscipienda — utendum est his iisdem regulis, sumendo scilicet eam partem ipsarum quae sufficit pro qualitate rei. Modus autem, seu regula, etiam in his omnibus particularibus actionibus est: omnia metiri ex Dei honore, nullo habito respectu ad proprias commoditates, maxime temporales, ut intentio semper in Deum recta sit, nec inflectatur ob aliquid terrenum.
paras.en: Finally, in other particular affairs — as in undertaking or not undertaking something — these same rules are to be used, taking from them that portion which suffices for the nature of the matter. And the method, or rule, in all these particular actions too is this: to measure everything by the honour of God, with no regard for one's own advantages, especially temporal ones, so that the intention be always straight toward God, and not bent aside by anything earthly.

kapitel.label: Cap. XXVI
kapitel.la_titel: De tempore triplici ad electionem recte faciendam
kapitel.en_titel: On the three times for making the election rightly

paras.la: Circa quartum, declaranda sunt tantum tria tempora electionis faciendae, quae habentur in libro exercitiorum: nam his bene cognitis, nihil fere aliud desiderari posse videtur. Tempora autem dicuntur, quia cum tales anima motiones sentit quales ibi describuntur, tunc aptum est tempus et opportunum electioni. Ac de primo quidem tempore pauca sunt dicenda: cum scilicet adeo clare constat de Dei voluntate, ut ne dubitari quidem de ea possit; pro cuius exemplo ponitur vocatio Matthaei et Pauli. Et quamvis iam non contingant eiusmodi vocationes ita miraculosae, tamen et legimus et videmus quasdam quae quodammodo ad eas videntur accedere, tanta claritate et satisfactione spiritus, tamque certa illustratione divinae voluntatis, ut ne in has quidem videatur cadere posse dubitatio. Sed haec vocatio nimis extraordinaria est, nec cadit sub regulam, et ideo nec a Deo petenda aut exspectanda est; et ob hanc etiam causam, cum tam raro accidat, non multum est in huius primi temporis consideratione insistendum, et obiter dumtaxat declarandum ei qui facit exercitia.
paras.en: As to the fourth point, only the three times for making the election need be explained, which are found in the book of the Exercises: for once these are well known, hardly anything else seems left to desire. They are called times because when the soul feels such movements as are described there, then the time is apt and opportune for the election. Of the first time, indeed, little need be said: namely, when God's will is so clearly evident that it cannot even be doubted; as examples of which are given the calling of Matthew and of Paul. And although such miraculous vocations no longer occur, still we both read of and see some which seem in a certain way to approach them, with such clarity and satisfaction of spirit, and so sure an illumination of the divine will, that not even in these does doubt seem able to find a place. But this vocation is too extraordinary, and does not fall under rule; and therefore it is neither to be asked of God nor to be waited for. For this reason too, since it happens so rarely, one need not dwell much on the consideration of this first time, and it should be explained only in passing to the one making the Exercises.

paras.la: Secundum igitur tempus est magis ordinarium: cum scilicet animus inspirationibus et motionibus internis agitur, iisque tam efficacibus, ut sine ullo intellectus discursu, aut fere nullo, voluntas feratur ad Dei servitutem et ad perfectionem.
paras.en: The second time, then, is more ordinary: namely, when the soul is moved by inward inspirations and motions, and these so efficacious that without any discourse of the understanding, or almost none, the will is borne toward the service of God and toward perfection.

paras.la: Tertium tempus est cum intellectus, ratiocinando et ponderando rationes pro una et altera parte, veritatem clarius aspicit, et veluti lumen voluntati praefert, ut voluntas id demum eligat quod, omnibus perpensis, melius fuerit iudicatum.
paras.en: The third time is when the understanding, by reasoning and weighing the arguments on either side, sees the truth more clearly, and carries a light, as it were, before the will, so that the will may at last choose what, all things weighed, has been judged the better.

kapitel.label: Cap. XXVII
kapitel.la_titel: Comparatio secundi temporis faciendae electionis cum tertio
kapitel.en_titel: Comparison of the second time of making the election with the third

paras.rub: Differentia voluntatis et intellectus in electione
paras.la: Itaque, etiamsi hae duae potentiae animae ita coniunctae sint, ut una sine altera in eligendo operari non possit, est tamen haec differentia: quod in primo et secundo tempore voluntas praecedit, intellectus vero sequitur, et ab ea trahitur sine ullo suo discursu aut cunctatione; in tertio autem praecedit intellectus ipse, tamque multas rationes voluntati proponit, ut eam extimulet et impellat in eam partem quam iudicat meliorem. Et quidem, hoc supposito quod motio illa sit immediate a Deo, sine dubio excellentior via est et altior, cum voluntas divinitus illustrata praecedit ac trahit intellectum: quia etiam Aristoteles, ut refert S. Thomas, ita ait, illis qui moventur secundum instinctum divinum non expedire consiliari secundum rationem humanam, quia moventur a meliori principio quam sit humana ratio. Sed posterior via, nempe per ratiocinationem et discursum, est securior et tutior.
paras.en: Now although these two powers of the soul are so conjoined that the one cannot operate in choosing without the other, there is nevertheless this difference: in the first and second times the will goes before, and the understanding follows, drawn by the will without any discourse or hesitation of its own; in the third, the understanding itself goes before, and sets so many reasons before the will as to spur it on and impel it toward the side it judges the better. And indeed, supposing that the motion is immediately from God, the former way is without doubt the more excellent and higher — when the will, divinely illumined, goes before and draws the understanding: for Aristotle too, as St. Thomas relates, says that for those who are moved by divine instinct it is not expedient to take counsel according to human reason, because they are moved by a better principle than human reason. But the latter way, namely through reasoning and discourse, is the safer and surer.

paras.rub: Quid in primo et secundo tempore
paras.la: Pro notitia autem primi et secundi temporis — quando scilicet, ut dictum est, anima afflatu divino permovetur — declarandum est exercenti se quid sit consolatio, et quid desolatio; de qua utraque agitur in tertia et quarta regula discernendi spiritus.
paras.en: For the understanding of the first and second times — when, as has been said, the soul is moved by the divine breath — it must be explained to the exercitant what consolation is, and what desolation; both of which are treated in the third and fourth Rules for the Discernment of Spirits.

paras.la: Haec autem consolatio non est habitus, sed veluti spiritualis passio data supernaturaliter, cuius natura est ut, dum praesens est, facile exerceantur actus virtutis, immo cum delectatione et gustu, et cum inflammatione affectus; contra vero facit ut opera carnis desipiant et insuavia videantur. Eius partes, vel modi, varii sunt: ut pax et quies quaedam interior, gaudium spirituale, lumen et clarior cognitio rerum divinarum, lachrymae, mentis elevatio in Deum, spes in Deo fixa, sensus rerum aeternarum, conversio ad coelestia, calor sancti amoris, et si qui sunt similes alii effectus vel affectus, qui sunt omnes a spiritu bono.
paras.en: This consolation is not a habit, but as it were a spiritual passion given supernaturally, whose nature is such that while it is present the acts of virtue are easily performed — indeed with delight and relish, and with an inflaming of the affections — while on the other hand it makes the works of the flesh lose their savour and appear unpleasing. Its parts, or modes, are various: a certain inward peace and quiet, spiritual joy, light and a clearer knowledge of divine things, tears, the raising of the mind to God, hope fixed in God, a feeling for eternal things, a turning toward the heavenly, the warmth of holy love, and any other like effects or affections — all of which are from the good spirit.

paras.la: Desolatio contra est tristitia, perturbatio animi, spes in rebus vel personis humanis, amor rerum inferiorum, ariditas, depressio et evagatio mentis in res huius mundi: quae sunt omnia a spiritu malo.
paras.en: Desolation, on the contrary, is sadness, disturbance of soul, hope placed in human things or persons, love of lower things, dryness, dejection, and the wandering of the mind among the things of this world: all of which are from the evil spirit.

paras.rub: Quae observanda in his temporibus electionem facturo
paras.la: Hoc igitur posito, ad cognoscendum utra ex duabus partibus, de quibus consultatur, magis placeat Deo, debet homo in seipso notare et animadvertere, quando sentit consolationem, ad quam partem eum inclinet consolatio et tranquillitas animae; et contra desolatio, cum eam sentit, ad quam partem eum magis inclinet. Et cum his temporibus contrariis videat se moveri ad contrarios effectus, debet pro certo habere nasci id ex principiis contrariis. Proprium enim est spiritus mali invadere animam tempore desolationis, eamque obruere pusillanimitate et tristitia et torpore; contra vero proprium est boni spiritus afferre animae laetitiam, et tempore laetitiae cum ea tractare et in eam influere. Uterque enim dat ex eo quod habet et quo abundat, ut constat ex regulis discretionis spirituum, praesertim quae huic secundae hebdomadae conveniunt: quae valde opportunae sunt hoc tempore, et sine illis fere ambulabitur in tenebris.
paras.en: This being laid down, in order to know which of the two alternatives under deliberation is more pleasing to God, a man should note and observe in himself, when he feels consolation, to which side the consolation and tranquillity of soul incline him; and, on the contrary, when he feels desolation, to which side it more inclines him. And when at these contrary times he sees himself moved to contrary effects, he should hold it for certain that this arises from contrary principles. For it is proper to the evil spirit to invade the soul in time of desolation and overwhelm it with faint-heartedness, sadness and torpor; and on the contrary it is proper to the good spirit to bring the soul joy, and in the time of joy to deal with it and flow into it. For each gives out of what he has and what he abounds in, as appears from the Rules for the Discernment of Spirits — especially those belonging to this Second Week — which are most timely now, and without which one will walk almost in darkness.

paras.rub: Praxis quaedam S. P. N. Ignatii
paras.la: Est etiam altera quaedam praxis huius rei, quam ponit P. N. Ignatius illa similitudine eius qui praesentat principi suo genus aliquod cibi, ut exploret quam ei arrideat. Sic anima, cum profunda humilitate et fervente amore ac desiderio gratificandi Deo, offerat ei diversis temporibus modo unam, modo alteram rem, observans quaenam ex illis a Deo magis accipiatur et admittatur, dicens semper: Domine, quid me vis facere? Quod non solum ore, aut leviori mentis affectu, sed toto corde, et multis cordibus, si tot haberet, ei dicendum et sentiendum est.
paras.en: There is also another practice in this matter, which Our Father Ignatius sets forth by the similitude of one who presents to his prince some kind of food, to see how it pleases him. So let the soul, with deep humility and fervent love and desire of pleasing God, offer him at different times now one thing, now another, observing which of them is more received and accepted by God, saying always: Lord, what would you have me do? And this must be said and felt not with the mouth only, or with a lighter movement of the mind, but with the whole heart — and with many hearts, if it had so many.

paras.rub: Optimum signum Dei vocantis ad perfectionem
paras.la: Porro inter alia indicia divinae voluntatis vocantis ad statum perfectiorem, illud est optimum: si anima sentit sibi promitti tantum pecuniae spiritualis, quantum necesse sit ad aedificandam hanc turrim evangelicae perfectionis; id est, si sentit labores huius vitae, qui aliis ita graves videntur, et ipsimet antea ita videri solebant, nunc leviores et faciliores reddi — sic ut voluntaria paupertas, vel abnegatio propriae voluntatis, vel castitatis observantia, et reliquarum virtutum exercitatio, iam non adeo gravis ei videatur; ut de seipso scribit S. Augustinus in libris Confessionum. Secundum est indicium, si hae cogitationes pergunt semper movere ad bonum: Satanas enim, licet ab initio dissimulet, in progressu tamen non potest diu se celare, quin incipiat depromere suum venenum.
paras.en: Further, among the other signs of the divine will calling to a more perfect state, this is the best: if the soul feels promised to it as much spiritual money as is needed to build this tower of evangelical perfection; that is, if it feels that the labours of this life, which seem so heavy to others, and used to seem so to itself, are now made lighter and easier — so that voluntary poverty, or the denial of one's own will, or the keeping of chastity, and the practice of the other virtues, no longer seem to it so burdensome; as St. Augustine writes of himself in the books of the Confessions. The second sign is if these thoughts continue always to move toward the good: for Satan, though he may dissemble at first, cannot in the course of things long conceal himself without beginning to bring out his poison.

paras.rub: De signis boni et mali spiritus
paras.la: Denique de eiusmodi signis boni vel mali spiritus optime et valde dilucide agitur in regulis discretionis spirituum posterioribus libri exercitiorum; agit etiam Gerson in libro de probatione spirituum, et Bonaventura de processu religionis, cap. 18.
paras.en: Finally, such signs of the good or evil spirit are treated excellently and very lucidly in the later Rules for the Discernment of Spirits in the book of the Exercises; Gerson also treats of them in his book on the testing of spirits, and Bonaventure in On the Progress of Religion, chapter 18.

paras.la: Atque haec hactenus de primo et secundo tempore electionis: in quo si ita constet de divina voluntate, ut anima plane confirmetur et stabiliatur, nec desideret maiorem certitudinem, potest hic conquiescere; sin vero non sufficiat, poterit progredi ad tertium tempus.
paras.en: So much, then, for the first and second times of the election. If in them the divine will becomes so evident that the soul is fully confirmed and settled, and desires no greater certainty, it may rest here; but if this does not suffice, it may go on to the third time.

kapitel.label: Cap. XXVIII
kapitel.la_titel: De modo priore et posteriore bonae electionis faciendae
kapitel.en_titel: On the first and second ways of making a good election

paras.la: Tertium tempus in libello exercitiorum duobus modis distinguitur, qui vocantur modus prior et modus posterior bonae electionis: prior sex punctis, posterior quatuor regulis continetur. Si ergo in priori non fiat electio, veniendum est ad posteriorem, qui est ultimus modus qui in hac materia tradi possit.
paras.en: The third time is divided in the little book of the Exercises into two ways, called the first and the second way of making a good election: the first is contained in six points, the second in four rules. If, then, the election is not made in the first, one must come to the second, which is the last way that can be given in this matter.

paras.rub: Quid in his modis eligendi requiratur
paras.la: Pro his autem duobus modis bene eligendi, sicut etiam omni tempore quo durat electio, requiritur tranquillitas animae: quoniam tempore turbationis non est locus electionis, cum scriptum sit: Ne festines in tempore obductionis (Eccli. 2). Quare qui hanc tranquillitatem in se non sentiret, satius esset ut progrediatur in meditationibus, donec tempestas deferveat et redeat serenitas: quoniam dum turbida est aqua, nihil in ea perspici potest.
paras.en: For these two ways of choosing well — as indeed for the whole time the election lasts — tranquillity of soul is required: for in a time of disturbance there is no place for election, since it is written: Make no haste in the time of clouds (Sir 2). Therefore one who did not feel this tranquillity in himself would do better to go on with the meditations until the storm cools and calm returns: for while the water is troubled, nothing can be seen in it.

paras.la: Supposita ergo hac tranquillitate, proponenda sunt ex una parte commoda, ex altera parte incommoda, provenientia ex ea re de qua agitur, et singula bene aestimanda et examinanda, ut videatur quaenam praeponderent.
paras.en: This tranquillity being supposed, there are to be set out on the one side the advantages, on the other the disadvantages, arising from the matter in question; and each is to be well weighed and examined, that it may be seen which preponderate.

paras.la: Tantum illud observandum et actuandum hic, quod supra attigimus: nempe has rationes, quae ad deliberationem adhibentur, debere omnes proficisci ex illo principio divini obsequii; nec admittendos esse in hac consultatione respectus humanos aut terrenas cogitationes.
paras.en: Only this must be observed and put into practice here, which we touched on above: that the reasons brought into the deliberation must all proceed from that principle of the divine service; and that no human considerations or earthly thoughts are to be admitted into this consultation.

paras.la: Notandum est etiam quod hi duo modi, quibus tertium tempus distinguitur, non solum tunc adhibendi sunt cum in secundo tempore nihil conclusum est; sed etiam, si facta sit electio, confert ad eam magis confirmandam et stabiliendam. Si enim anima certa esset quod illa motio secundi temporis esset a Deo, sine dubio nihil ei esset amplius requirendum; sed quia angelus satanae transfigurat se aliquando in angelum lucis (2 Cor. 11), ideo haec generalis regula esse debet: valde periculosum esse cum homo vult se gubernare tantum per motus voluntatis et sensus quosdam interiores, non adhibendo considerationem debitam. Et ideo probatio et examen fieri debet per lumen: quia, ut dicit Apostolus, omne quod manifestatur lumen est (Ephes. 5, 13). Hoc autem lumen, post lumen fidei, est etiam ipsa humana ratio — adiuta tamen et illuminata lumine fidei — quae ipsa quoque a Deo est; et non potest unum repugnare alteri, quia necessarium est ut verum vero consonum sit.
paras.en: It should also be noted that these two ways, into which the third time is divided, are to be used not only when nothing has been concluded in the second time; but even if the election has been made, this serves to confirm and settle it the more. For if the soul were certain that that motion of the second time was from God, doubtless nothing more would need to be required of it; but because the angel of Satan sometimes transfigures himself into an angel of light (2 Cor 11), this must be the general rule: that it is very dangerous for a man to wish to govern himself only by movements of the will and certain inward feelings, without applying due consideration. And therefore the testing and examination must be made by light: for, as the Apostle says, everything that is made manifest is light (Eph 5:13). And this light, after the light of faith, is also human reason itself — aided, however, and illumined by the light of faith — which also is itself from God; and the one cannot contradict the other, for truth must needs be consonant with truth.

paras.la: Itaque hoc etiam signum est spiritus mali: quando refugit hoc examen, quia amat tenebras, et non vult venire ad lucem, ut non arguantur opera eius (Ioan. 3, 20). Hanc igitur ob causam hic modus eligendi securior est: quia ratio, fide illuminata et Ecclesiae catholicae doctrina instructa, suo officio fungitur; et cum totas vires suas, et quicquid potest, exponat in inquirenda Dei voluntate, fideliter facit quod in ipsa est.
paras.en: This too, then, is a sign of the evil spirit: when he shrinks from this examination, because he loves darkness and will not come to the light, lest his works be reproved (John 3:20). For this reason this way of choosing is the safer: because reason, illumined by faith and instructed by the doctrine of the Catholic Church, performs its office; and since it spends all its strength, and whatever it can, in searching out the will of God, it faithfully does what lies in it.
paras.note: Margin: 'Ex reg. 13 ad motus animae discernendos.'

paras.la: Si vero ad has rationes adiungatur etiam experientia quam quis habeat suae infirmitatis — ut manifeste sentiat salutem suam in saeculo exponi magno discrimini — non est dubium quin securius etiam res procedat.
paras.en: And if to these reasons is joined the experience a man has of his own weakness — so that he plainly feels his salvation in the world to be exposed to great hazard — there is no doubt that the matter proceeds all the more surely.

paras.la: Quod si praeterea rationes istae confirmentur per aliqua signa secundi temporis, quae superius diximus — nempe pacis, consolationis aut gustus — tum vero anima maiorem etiam satisfactionem et claritatem accipit.
paras.en: And if, moreover, these reasons are confirmed by some of the signs of the second time which we mentioned above — namely peace, consolation or relish — then indeed the soul receives even greater satisfaction and clarity.

paras.rub: Quid si secundo tempore fit inclinatio
paras.la: Quaeret aliquis quid faciendum sit, si forte contingat ut secundo tempore in aliquam rem inclinemur, tertio vero tempore in alteram ei contrariam vel dissimilem. Respondemus esse diligenter rem examinandam per regulas discernendi spiritus et per rectam rationem, et aestimandum pondus rerum moventium utroque modo. Quod si constaret clare quod ratio astipulatur electioni tertii temporis, securius est eam sequi: quia non est certum an motio illa secundi temporis sit a Deo, et tunc maxime cum ratio aliud suadet. Contra vero, si rationes quae tertio tempore movent essent debiles, motiones autem secundi temporis, bene examinatae iuxta regulas, videntur esse a Deo, et recta ratio eis non repugnat, tota electio secundi temporis est praeferenda: licet enim prius clare non constaret per eam de Dei voluntate, tamen, rebus melius agitatis et discussis, accedente rationis testimonio, potest fieri ut constet.
paras.en: Someone will ask what is to be done if it should happen that in the second time we incline toward one thing, and in the third time toward another contrary or unlike it. We answer that the matter must be diligently examined by the Rules for the Discernment of Spirits and by right reason, and the weight of what moves us in each way assessed. If it were clearly established that reason supports the election of the third time, it is safer to follow it: for it is not certain that the motion of the second time is from God, and least of all when reason counsels otherwise. On the contrary, if the reasons that move in the third time were weak, while the motions of the second time, well examined according to the rules, appear to be from God, and right reason is not against them, the election of the second time is altogether to be preferred: for though God's will was not previously made clearly evident through it, still, when things have been better weighed and sifted, with the testimony of reason added, it may come to be evident.

kapitel.label: Cap. XXIX
kapitel.la_titel: De praxi et ordine electionis
kapitel.en_titel: On the practice and order of the election

paras.la: Restat nunc ultimum: nempe tota praxis et ordo proponendi electionem, et manuducendi eum qui facit exercitia. In primis igitur hoc valde notandum est, quod etiam supra indicavimus: iam tum ab initio huius secundae hebdomadae incipere disponi animam per meditationem illam de Regno Christi, quae mentem erigit a terrenis et fluxis ad Salvatoris imitationem desiderandam; quae quidem dispositio alenda est semper deinceps in eo qui se exercet, excitando eum et dirigendo ad id quod perfectius est per reliquas meditationes, ut Nativitatis, Circuncisionis et alias, in quibus ita instruendus est ut concipiat desiderium assimilandi se Filio Dei, et praeterea quam maximam possit erga eum gratitudinem, qui tanta nobis dedit et tanta pro nobis fecit. In hac autem contemplatione de Regno Christi existimandum non est verba illa — attestans coram infinita bonitate tua etc. — voti vim habere, cum annotatione decima quarta ex viginti sit peculiaris admonitio, ne quis vacans exercitiis voto se facile obstringat.
paras.en: There now remains the last point: the whole practice and order of proposing the election and of leading by the hand the one making the Exercises. First of all, then, this is much to be noted, which we also indicated above: that already from the beginning of this Second Week the soul begins to be disposed by that meditation on the Kingdom of Christ, which lifts the mind from earthly and fleeting things to the desire of imitating the Saviour; and this disposition is to be nourished continually thereafter in the exercitant, stirring and directing him toward what is more perfect through the remaining meditations — the Nativity, the Circumcision, and the others — in which he is to be so instructed that he conceive the desire of likening himself to the Son of God, and moreover the greatest gratitude he can toward him who has given us so much and done so much for us. In this contemplation on the Kingdom of Christ, however, the words — protesting before your infinite goodness, etc. — are not to be thought to have the force of a vow, since in the fourteenth of the twenty Annotations there is a special warning that no one engaged in the Exercises should lightly bind himself by vow.

paras.rub: Quarta vel quinta die inchoanda meditatio electionis
paras.la: Deinde quarto vel quinto die inchoantur meditationes electionis, per illud exercitium pueri Iesu cum remansit in templo: in quo, ut dicitur in libro exercitiorum, coepit dare exemplum huius evangelicae perfectionis, quando, patre putativo et naturali matre relictis, voluit occupari in iis quae aeterni Patris essent.
paras.en: Then on the fourth or fifth day the meditations of the election are begun, with that exercise of the boy Jesus when he remained in the temple: in which, as is said in the book of the Exercises, he began to give the example of this evangelical perfection when, leaving his putative father and his natural mother, he chose to be occupied in the things that were his eternal Father's.
paras.note: Margin: 'Praeludio circa electionem statuum.'

paras.la: Igitur, ad disponendam animam electioni faciendae, post hanc meditationem datur primo exercitium duorum vexillorum, deinde eodem die meditatio de tribus hominum classibus: quae ad hoc tendit, ut iuxta eas qui in exercitiis est se examinet, et cognoscat affectum suum erga res mundanas; et si in prima vel secunda classe se deprehenderit, conetur sibi vim facere, ut se transferat in tertiam.
paras.en: In order, then, to dispose the soul for making the election, after this meditation there is given first the exercise of the Two Standards, then on the same day the meditation on the Three Classes of Men: which aims at this, that the one in the Exercises examine himself by them and come to know his affection toward worldly things; and if he finds himself in the first or second class, that he strive to do himself violence, so as to bring himself over into the third.

paras.la: Ad maiorem autem intelligentiam harum trium classium, notandum est hoc in omnibus supponi: modum illum quo pecunia illa acquisita est non esse illicitum, ita ut obliget ad restitutionem.
